name: Filippo Menczer
title: Luddy Distinguished Professor; Director, Observatory on Social Media
research area: Computational Social Science; Misinformation; Network/Web Science
short bio: Leads OSoMe/CNetS to model and counter online manipulation at scale; recent highlights include election to the 2024 AAAS Fellows class and a large slate of OSoMe/CNetS summer publications on bot detection and misinformation dynamics.
long bio: Filippo Menczer (born May 16, 1965) is an American and Italian academic and University Distinguished Professor at Indiana University’s Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, where he directs the Observatory on Social Media (OSoMe). His research focuses on web science, social networks, misinformation, social bots, and the dynamics of information diffusion in complex networks. Menczer has made influential contributions to the study of echo chambers, information virality, search engine bias, and online manipulation, and he developed widely used tools such as Botometer and Hoaxy to detect bots and track the spread of low-credibility content. His work has helped uncover disinformation campaigns, analyze political polarization, and study the impact of online misinformation on issues such as elections and COVID-19 vaccination. A fellow of the ACM, he has received major honors including an NSF CAREER Award and multiple international fellowships. He is also co-author of the textbook A First Course in Network Science and has held numerous editorial and leadership roles in the network science and web research communities.

name: Kristina Lerman
title: Professor
research area: Humana AI Alignment; Bias & Fairness; Technology & Society
short bio: Network scientist with two decades of social web research; joined Luddy in 2025, with current work probing how AI chatbots may exacerbate mental health risks and how to align human AI systems for public benefit.
long bio: Kristina Lerman is an American network scientist and professor whose research focuses on social computing, complex social networks, and machine-learning methods to understand information spread, algorithmic bias, and social behavior online. She is a Professor of Informatics at Indiana University’s Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, and formerly spent many years as a Senior Principal Scientist at the USC Information Sciences Institute and Research Professor in USC’s Viterbi School of Engineering. Lerman’s work explores how algorithms and social platforms shape what people see, how information propagates, and the digital vulnerabilities that can lead to manipulation, polarization, and mental-health harms. She also develops methods to audit and correct biases in data and AI systems to create fairer socially-embedded technologies. Her highly cited research includes studies on social contagion, bias and fairness in machine learning, and the dynamics of news and misinformation on platforms such as Twitter and Digg. Lerman is recognized as a Fellow of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence and her work has been covered by major media outlets

name: Johan Bollen
title: Professor; Chair of Informatics
research area: Computational Social Science; Well being; Science of Science
short bio: Johan Bollen is a scientist known for his work on complex systems, computational social science, and scholarly impact metrics. He is a Professor of Informatics and Cognitive Science at Indiana University Bloomington and a fellow at Wageningen University’s SparcS Institute. His research explores how large-scale social media data can be used to measure public mood, predict financial markets, and assess scientific impact, including a well-known study linking Twitter sentiment to stock market movements. Bollen has published over 100 papers, holds two patents, and has received significant research funding from major institutions such as the NIH, NSF, NASA, and the Mellon Foundation.
long bio: Johan Bollen is a scientist specializing in complex systems, computational social science, and the science of science. He is a Professor of Informatics and Cognitive Science at Indiana University Bloomington and a fellow at Wageningen University’s SparcS Institute in the Netherlands. His research examines the relationship between social media and socio-economic phenomena, including financial markets, public health, and social well-being, and he is particularly known for linking Twitter mood data to stock market trends. Bollen has also contributed significantly to the development of alternative scholarly impact metrics based on usage data rather than citations. He has published over 100 papers, received more than 21,000 citations, and holds two patents related to impact assessment and economic trend prediction. His work has been funded by major organizations such as the NIH, NSF, NASA, and the Mellon Foundation, and he has also taught courses on collective intelligence, data mining, and information retrieval.

name: Alessandro Flammini
title: Professor
department: Informatics (Center for Complex Networks & Systems Research)
research area: Complex Networks; Information Diffusion; Social Computing
short bio: Studies diffusion, polarization, and the role of bots in online ecosystems; recent work refines network based indicators to track coordinated behavior and misinformation flows.
long bio: Alessandro Flammini is a Professor of Informatics at Indiana University’s Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, where he also serves as Department Chair of Informatics and holds an adjunct appointment in physics. His background is in statistical physics, and his research focuses on complex networks and computational social science, including how information spreads in social media and how online systems behave as socio-technical networks. Flammini has held research positions at institutions such as the University of Cambridge, MIT’s Ralph Parsons Lab, and the University of Lausanne prior to joining Indiana University. He has collaborated on influential work on social bots, misinformation, and online information diffusion, with many highly cited publications in network science and computational social systems. Flammini is regularly recognized as a leading researcher, having been listed among top artificial intelligence scholars for his impact in the field. His work spans both theoretical and applied aspects of network analysis, contributing to understanding topics from human-bot interactions to complex patterns of online communication and polarization.

name: Gabriele Guidi
title: Professor; Informatics Graduate Director; Director, Virtual World Heritage Lab
research area: Digital Heritage; 3D Digitization; Sensor Fusion; VR/AR Museums
short bio: Pioneers high fidelity 3D acquisition and digital twins for museums; recent projects integrate active/passive sensors and large scale pipelines for cultural heritage and exhibition curation; Editor in Chief of *Studies in Digital Heritage*.
long bio: Gabriele Guidi is a Full Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington and Director of the Virtual World Heritage Lab, where he also leads the Virtual Heritage Informatics Ph.D. track. He received his M.S. in Electronic Engineering from the University of Florence and his Ph.D. from the University of Bologna, and previously served on the faculty at the Polytechnic University of Milan before joining Indiana University in 2021. Guidi’s research focuses on three-dimensional (3D) imaging, digitization, and data processing techniques applied to cultural heritage, including sensor fusion, geometric processing, and digital replicas of artifacts and sites. He has helped pioneer large-scale 3D digitization projects of artworks and archaeological structures and develops methods for integrating active and passive 3D technologies for cultural heritage applications. Guidi is editor-in-chief of Studies in Digital Heritage and his work supports applications in museums, conservation, and virtual/augmented reality for cultural content. His scholarly contributions have advanced the use of 3D technologies in digital humanities, museum informatics, and cultural heritage preservation

name: Patrick C. Shih
title: Associate Professor; Director of Graduate Studies (Data Science)
research area: HCI; Health Informatics; Social/Community Computing; Animal Computer Interaction
short bio: Designs sociotechnical systems to support health and vulnerable populations; recent work includes NSF funded research on epilepsy information sharing and community based mobility and care coordination initiatives.
long bio: Patrick C. Shih is an Associate Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, where he also serves as Director of Graduate Studies for Data Science and co-director of the Animal Informatics MS/PhD track. His research focuses on designing and evaluating sociotechnical systems to support health, well-being, and underserved communities, and includes work in human–computer interaction, social computing, health informatics, and animal-computer interaction. Shih directs the Societal Computing Lab, which explores community-centered technology design and mechanisms for improving welfare and empathy through technology. He earned his Ph.D. in Information and Computer Science from the University of California, Irvine, and previously held positions at Penn State’s College of Information Sciences and Technology. Shih’s work spans a range of applied and theoretical projects—such as technology to support physical activity, community care systems, and digital tools for health and social support—with many publications in top HCI conferences and journals. He has received recognition including an NSF CAREER Award and ACM senior membership for his contributions to computing research.

name: Katie A. Siek
title: Professor
research area: HCI; Ubiquitous Computing; Digital Health & Equity
short bio: Leads community engaged health informatics across reproductive health, older adults, and digital wellbeing; recent service includes ACM DEI Council (2025-2027) and computing futures policy activities.
long bio: Katie A. Siek is a Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, where she conducts research in human-computer interaction, health informatics, and ubiquitous computing. Her work focuses on how sociotechnical systems and pervasive technologies can improve health, wellness, and well-being outside traditional clinical settings, often through mobile, wearable, and ambient computing solutions. She has received significant research support from agencies such as the NIH, NSF, and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and has earned awards including a five-year NSF CAREER award, an IU Trustees Teaching Award, and a NCWIT Undergraduate Research Mentoring Award. Siek also serves in leadership roles in the computing research community, including on the Computing Research Association Board and the Computing Community Consortium Council. Her scholarship is widely cited in areas such as consumer health informatics and pervasive healthcare, and she mentors many students on projects that bridge technology with underserved populations and health equity. Prior to her current position, she was a professor at the University of Colorado Boulder and holds a Ph.D. and M.S. from Indiana University and a B.S. in computer science from Eckerd College.

name: Jisun An
title: Assistant Professor
research area: AI for Social Good; NLP; Media Analytics
short bio: Builds AI/NLP to study media bias, framing, polarization, and online hate; recent publications evaluate when LLMs can substitute for human annotators on implicit hate and track public sentiment on generative AI.
long bio: Jisun An is an Assistant Professor at the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington, where she is part of the Social Data and AI (SODA) Lab. Her research develops AI and natural language processing methods to understand, predict, and influence online human behavior and address societal challenges such as media bias, polarization, online hate, and health-related behavior. An’s work spans computational social science, news and social media analytics, and the social impacts of AI, with many widely-cited publications on topics like news engagement, political communication, and online misinformation. Before joining Indiana University, she was a faculty member at Singapore Management University and a scientist at the Qatar Computing Research Institute. She holds a Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Cambridge and her research has been published in major venues across social computing and NLP. An’s work also includes empirical studies on generative AI perception and techniques for profiling and bias detection in online media.

name: Haewoon Kwak
title: Associate Professor
research area: Computational Social Science; Social Computing; Platform Dynamics
short bio: Coleads SODA Lab; widely cited work reframed Twitter as an information network; recent research models toxicity, polarization, and media ecosystems using modern NLP and large scale data.
long bio: Haewoon Kwak is an Associate Professor at the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington, where he co-leads the Social Data and AI (SODA) Lab studying social phenomena with large-scale data and computational tools. His research sits at the intersection of network science, machine learning, and computational social science, focusing on social media dynamics, news media, online behavior, and information quality. Kwak is widely cited for his influential work, including the highly cited paper “What is Twitter, a social network or news media?”, which has been referenced over 10,000 times. His research covers diverse topics such as toxicity and hate in online discussions, media bias and consumption, personas in social networks, and the structure and dynamics of large online platforms. Before joining Indiana University in 2023, he held academic and research positions at Singapore Management University and the Qatar Computing Research Institute. Kwak’s work has been featured in major media outlets and he serves on program committees for leading conferences in computer science and computational social science.

name: Elizabeth Kaziunas
title: Assistant Professor
research area: HCI; CSCW; Health Informatics; AI Ethics
short bio: Examines lived experiences of health datafication and AI/ML in care settings; recent work from AI Now and Luddy considers algorithmic care, data justice, and equity in clinical decision support.
long bio: Elizabeth Kaziunas is an Assistant Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington’s Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, where she teaches in the Human-Computer Interaction and Design program. Her research sits at the intersection of human-computer interaction (HCI), computer-supported cooperative work (CSCW), and health informatics, focusing on the social and organizational contexts of health information systems and the lived experiences of health datafication. As an interpretivist scholar, she combines ethnographic methods with human-centered design to explore how people engage with health information technologies and the broader implications of data-driven systems on care and society. Prior to her faculty role at IU, Kaziunas was a Research Lead on the Algorithmic Care Project and a postdoctoral researcher at the AI Now Institute, where she investigated the social impacts of AI and machine learning in healthcare settings. She holds a Ph.D. from the University of Michigan’s School of Information and advanced degrees from Syracuse University, Yale University, and Macalester College. Her work is well-cited in fields related to sociotechnical systems, health data practices, and HCI research.

name: David J. Wild
title: Professor
department: Informatics (Integrative Data Science Lab; Crisis Technologies Innovation Lab)
research area: Integrative Data Science; AI & Drug Discovery; Crisis Tech; Privacy/Security
short bio: Founded IU's graduate Data Science programs; current work spans generative AI and crisis tech; launched the RedLab accelerator and leads CTIL efforts translating AI to first responder and emergency workflows.
long bio: David J. Wild is a Professor in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington, where he specializes in data science and artificial intelligence applied to complex real-world problems such as healthcare, drug discovery, emergency response, cybersecurity, and privacy. He founded and directs research initiatives including the Integrative Data Science Lab and RedLab, which focus on leveraging AI and data technologies for crisis and disaster response, and he also serves as CEO of the AI company Konnex.ai. Wild has an academic background in computing science and computational drug discovery, and he worked in the pharmaceutical industry before joining IU in 2004, where he also helped establish and grow graduate data science programs. His research contributions span data science, digital health, big data analytics, semantic technologies, and cheminformatics, with many publications and leadership in interdisciplinary research. He has founded startups such as Data2Discovery, a company pioneering AI for drug discovery, and serves as founding editor of the Journal of Cheminformatics. Wild’s work bridges academia, industry, and entrepreneurship, aiming to apply informatics and AI for societal impact in health and emergency management contexts.

name: Staša Milojević
title: Professor; Director, Center for Complex Networks & Systems Research
research area: Science of Science; Scientometrics; Network Science
short bio: Models team formation, career dynamics, and knowledge production; recent studies quantify workforce churn, interdisciplinarity, and the visibility of scholars across platforms.
long bio: Staša Milojević is a Professor of Informatics in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington, where she also directs the Center for Complex Networks and Systems Research and is a core faculty member of the Cognitive Science program. Her research focuses on the science of science, seeking to understand the dynamics of scientific knowledge production, collaboration, and the evolution of research systems through quantitative models that draw on network science, sociology, economics, and history. She uses theoretical and empirical methods to uncover fundamental principles that govern how science works as a heterogeneous, socially embedded system. Milojević’s highly cited work has appeared in leading journals, and she serves on the editorial boards of Scientometrics, BioScience, and Journal of Altmetrics as well as being Associate Editor for Quantitative Science Studies and Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics. She earned her Ph.D. in Information Studies from the University of California, Los Angeles, and her research contributes to understanding team science, interdisciplinarity, and changing patterns in scientific careers and productivity. Her scholarship integrates perspectives from information science and network analysis to advance the study of how scientific ideas and collaborations emerge and evolve.

name: Justin N. Wood
title: Associate Professor
research area: Reverse Engineering Biological Intelligence; Vision; Reinforcement Learning
short bio: Combines controlled rearing of newborn animals with parallel training of AI agents to uncover learning mechanisms that give rise to perception and cognition; current goals target end to end agents that mimic newborn learning.
long bio: Justin N. Wood is an Associate Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, with affili­ations in Psychological and Brain Sciences and Cognitive Science programs. His research explores the origins and nature of intelligence by combining controlled experiments on newborn animals (such as chicks) with computational models and AI systems to understand how learning and cognitive abilities emerge from experience. His lab uses innovative controlled-rearing virtual environments to compare biological learning in animals with artificial agents trained under similar conditions, aiming to reverse-engineer intelligence. Wood has a strong publication record in psychology, neuroscience, and AI, and his work includes highly cited studies on numerical cognition, visual perception, and object recognition across species and models. He has received research support from organizations such as the National Science Foundation and the James S. McDonnell Foundation. Wood’s interdisciplinary work spans psychology, computational neuroscience, and machine learning, bridging biological and artificial learning systems.

name: Nathan Ensmenger
title: Associate Professor
research area: History of Computing & AI; Software Workforce; Computing & Environment
short bio: Historian examining the social/cultural history of software and AI, masculinities in programming, and the environmental history of computing; recent campus projects explore public interest AI applications.
long bio: Nathan Ensmenger is a Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, and a core faculty member of the History and Philosophy of Science program. His research examines the social, cultural, and historical dimensions of computing and information technologies, including how professions, expertise, and organizational practices have shaped computing from its early days to the present. Ensmenger is the author of The Computer Boys Take Over: Computers, Programmers, and the Politics of Technical Expertise and has published widely on topics such as programming culture, workplace automation, and the historical development of tech professions. He also studies gender and diversity in computing, investigating how social and institutional forces influence who participates in computing fields. Ensmenger’s scholarship bridges history, sociology, and informatics, and he frequently serves on editorial boards and in leadership roles in the history of technology community. His work is widely cited and used in both academic research and teaching to contextualize computing within broader social and historical frameworks.

name: David Crandall
title: Luddy Professor
short bio: Leads research on visual recognition, video understanding, and vision language learning; recent work targets egocentric perception and open world robustness.
long bio: David Crandall is a Professor of Informatics and Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research spans computer vision, machine learning, and social computing, with a focus on developing algorithms that understand visual and multimodal data and how these technologies interact with society. Crandall’s work includes research on image analysis, deep learning, computational social science, and large-scale data mining, often emphasizing ethical and societal implications of AI systems. He has published extensively in top conferences and journals and is known for contributions that bridge technical innovation with real-world applications. Crandall also actively engages in efforts to benchmark and evaluate machine learning systems and has received funding from major agencies such as the National Science Foundation and DARPA. His interdisciplinary work contributes to both foundational AI research and practical systems for understanding complex visual and social data.

name: Saul Blanco
title: Assistant Professor
research area: Theoretical Computer Science; Algorithms; Learning Theory
short bio: Develops theory for algorithms and machine learning, with focus on efficiency and guarantees.
long bio: Saúl A. Blanco is an Assistant Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington and holds an adjunct appointment in Mathematics, where he teaches and conducts research in theoretical computer science and discrete mathematics. His research interests include combinatorics, discrete math, theoretical computer science, and applications of AI and machine learning to structural pattern problems. Blanco has published work on topics such as prefix-reversal graphs, algebraic combinatorics, and pseudo-random number generation, as well as interdisciplinary work involving machine learning and social media data analysis. He contributes to conferences and journals in both theoretical and applied domains, including papers presented at ISSAC, AAAI, and research on optimization and combinatorial structures. His work also spans topics in computer science education, such as understanding feedback effects on student learning. Blanco is part of Luddy School’s faculty engaged in foundational computing research, blending mathematical rigor with computational applications.

name: M. (Memo) Dalkilic
title: Professor
short bio: Builds data centric AI and scalable data systems for scientific discovery and health.
long bio: Mehmet M. “Memo” Dalkilic is an Associate Professor of Computer Science in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington, and also holds an adjunct appointment in the Department of Statistics. He is known for designing and teaching foundational computing courses such as the large-enrollment I101 Introduction to Informatics class and creating graduate and introductory classes to broaden participation in computer science. His research spans data science, data mining, and applied artificial intelligence, allowing him to address diverse problems across domains including astronomy, climate change, and public transportation. Dalkilic has also contributed to bioinformatics and consulting work with the Naval Surface Warfare Center, and his work has been supported by agencies like the NSF and NIH. He earned his Ph.D. in computer science from Indiana University and has played a key role in developing computing curricula that support student success and community building. Outside of academia, he enjoys reading, playing piano, and spending time with his Alaskan malamute.

name: Jiangpeng He
title: Distinguished Professor
short bio: Creates methods to study gene family evolution and speciation; recent work integrates ML with comparative genomics.
long bio: Jiangpeng He is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, where he also contributes to AI and computer vision research. He completed his Ph.D. in Electrical and Computer Engineering at Purdue University and was previously a Postdoctoral Associate at MIT working on smart rehabilitation robotics before joining IU. His research focuses on computer vision, deep learning, continual learning, and visual recognition systems, with applications that include food image analysis and incremental learning for real-world classification problems. He has published extensively in top computer vision and machine learning venues and has a growing citation record reflecting impactful work on topics such as class-incremental learning and image-based dietary assessment. Jiangpeng He’s recent research includes work accepted to major conferences such as CVPR and IEEE journals, and he frequently explores practical and theoretical advances in visual AI. He also seeks collaboration and supervises graduate students in areas related to AI for healthcare and long-tail learning problems.

name: Mohsen Heidari
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Focuses on video understanding and foundation model approaches for biomedical imaging.
long bio: Mohsen Heidari is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington, where he is also affiliated with the IU Quantum Science and Engineering Center and the NSF Center for Science of Information. He earned his Ph.D. in Electrical Engineering and an M.Sc. in Mathematics from the University of Michigan, and before joining IU he held positions at Purdue University as a visiting assistant professor and postdoctoral research associate. His research interests span quantum computing and algorithms, theoretical machine learning, and classical and quantum information theory, focusing on foundational computational problems and learning from quantum data. He has published work on topics such as quantum neural networks, regret bounds in learning algorithms, and information‐theoretic analysis of learning and communication systems. He teaches courses in algorithm design and analysis as well as quantum computing at both undergraduate and graduate levels. His scholarship bridges theoretical computer science and emerging quantum technologies, with active research supporting advances in scalable quantum and classical learning methods.

name: Thai Le
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Explores quantum algorithms alongside classical ML theory for more efficient learning.
long bio: Thai Le is an Associate Professor of Informatics and Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, where he also serves as Director of Graduate Studies for the Computer Science department. His research focuses on artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data science, particularly in the development of robust, scalable learning algorithms and intelligent systems. Le’s work includes contributions to adversarial machine learning, trust and safety in AI, reinforcement learning, and deep learning, with applications across autonomous systems and real-world decision making. He has published extensively in top AI and machine learning conferences and journals and has received competitive research funding for his work. In addition to his research, Le is active in teaching core computing courses and mentoring graduate students. His interdisciplinary work bridges theoretical foundations of AI with practical systems and societal impact.

name: David Leake
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Builds NLP methods to detect harms and misinformation; recent projects model implicit hate and state aligned narrative influence.
long bio: David Leake is a Professor of Informatics and Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, where he also serves as Associate Dean for Research. His research focuses on artificial intelligence, especially in the areas of case-based reasoning, knowledge management, and intelligent decision support systems, with applications in law, healthcare, engineering, and sustainability. Leake has published extensively on computational models that leverage past cases to inform new problem solving and has contributed foundational work to retrieval, learning, and explanation methods in AI. He has also been involved in interdisciplinary research on organizational learning and human-AI collaboration, exploring how AI systems can augment human expertise. In addition to his scholarly work, Leake teaches courses in AI and leads initiatives to integrate AI into broader research and education at IU. His work has been supported by major funding agencies including the National Science Foundation and the Department of Defense.

name: Byung-Cheol Min
title: Professor
short bio: Works on case based reasoning, explanation, and introspective agents; Editor Emeritus of *AI Magazine*.
long bio: Byung-Cheol (“B.C.”) Min is a Professor with a joint appointment in the Department of Computer Science and the Department of Intelligent Systems Engineering at the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington, having joined IU in Fall 2025. He directs the SMART Laboratory (Smart Machine And Robotics Technology Lab), where his research focuses on robotics, human-robot interaction, robot learning, and multi-robot systems, including distributed control, reinforcement learning, and generative AI for real-world challenges. Before joining IU, Min was a faculty member at Purdue University from 2015 to 2025, serving as assistant and associate professor and directing the Applied AI Research Center. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer and Information Technology with a specialization in robotics from Purdue University and completed postdoctoral research at Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute. Min’s research contributions span human-robot teams, distributed multi-agent systems, and learning methods that allow robots to collaborate with each other and with humans in dynamic environments. He has received significant recognitions including the NSF CAREER Award and multiple faculty honors, and he has published extensively on robotics and intelligent systems.

name: Christopher Raphael
title: Professor
short bio: Builds resilient autonomous and field robots; recent work integrates learning with human robot teaming.
long bio: Christopher Chris Raphael is a Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, where he also contributes to research and teaching in algorithms and theoretical computer science. His research focuses on design and analysis of algorithms, particularly for big data, streaming data, optimization, and machine learning, with applications spanning social data analysis, networks, and distributed systems. Raphael has published widely on algorithmic models for processing massive datasets efficiently and on linking theoretical insights with practical performance in real-world computing problems. He teaches core and advanced courses in algorithms and data structures, and his work has influenced both foundational CS research and applied data science methods. Before joining IU, he held faculty positions at other major research universities and has collaborated broadly across computer science and engineering. His contributions include both foundational theory and impactful interdisciplinary applications that help bridge rigorous CS theory with emerging data-intensive domains.

name: Gregory Rawlins
title: Professor
short bio: Applies AI to music understanding/performance; leads projects on score alignment and analysis at scale.
long bio: Gregory Rawlins is an Associate Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research centers on human–computer interaction (HCI), computer–supported cooperative work (CSCW), and participatory design, with a focus on how people engage with technology in everyday and work contexts. Rawlins investigates topics such as collaborative systems, digital work practices, and design methods that support effective teamwork and user empowerment. He teaches courses related to interaction design, qualitative research methods, and user experience, and he mentors students in both undergraduate and graduate programs. Rawlins’s work has been published in top HCI and CSCW venues, and he actively contributes to the research community through service and leadership roles. His interdisciplinary scholarship bridges computing, design, and social sciences to better understand technology’s role in social and organizational settings.

name: Chung-chieh Shan
title: Associate Professor (Emeritus)
short bio: Educator and author on NLP and general purpose AI systems.
long bio: Chung-chieh Shan is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University’s Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. He specializes in programming languages, probabilistic programming, and the semantics of computation, and his research involves developing foundations and tools for reasoning about programs and inference systems. Shan holds a Ph.D. in Computer Science from Harvard University and has published widely in top venues on topics such as probabilistic programming, symbolic disintegration, and functional programming techniques. He co-authored the book Continuations and Natural Language and has received teaching awards, including the IU Trustees Teaching Award in 2024, recognizing his excellence in the classroom. In addition to core research, he teaches courses ranging from introduction to computer science to advanced programming languages and probabilistic programming. Shan is active in the broader programming languages community, serving on program committees and contributing to international conferences in his field.

name: Haixu Tang
title: Associate Professor
short bio: Bridges programming languages and probabilistic models to enable explainable statistical AI.
long bio: Haixu Tang is a Professor of Informatics and Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington’s Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, where he also serves as Director of the Cyberinfrastructure Development Program. His research spans bioinformatics, computational biology, and data science, with a focus on developing algorithms and systems for understanding biological data, including genome analysis and integrative computational methods. Tang’s work includes contributions to sequence analysis, machine learning applications in biology, and scalable computational frameworks to support complex data-driven biological research. He has published extensively in top journals and conferences, and his research has been funded by major agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the National Science Foundation (NSF). Tang also plays leadership roles in advancing computational infrastructure and training, helping to build community resources and curricula for the life sciences. His interdisciplinary approach bridges biology, informatics, and computational science to tackle fundamental problems in biological data interpretation and discovery.

name: Zoran Tiganj
title: Professor
short bio: Develops algorithms for proteomics and secure genomic computing; recent efforts include privacy preserving discovery of genomic markers and scalable omics pipelines.
long bio: Zoran Tiganj is an Associate Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington’s Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, with affiliations in cognitive science and psychology. His research focuses on cognitive modeling, memory and learning, and the development of computational models of human cognition, often using mathematical and neural network approaches to understand how memory works over time. He studies topics such as temporal representations in memory, decision making, and how experience shapes learning and recall across contexts. Tiganj teaches courses in cognitive science, computational modeling, and research methods, and mentors students pursuing interdisciplinary work at the intersection of psychology and computation. His work is widely published in cognitive science, neuroscience, and interdisciplinary journals, contributing to theoretical and empirical understanding of how the brain encodes and retrieves information. Tiganj’s research bridges experimental psychology with formal and computational theories to illuminate the mechanisms of memory and cognition.

name: Yijie Wang
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Models sequence memory and time in neural circuits to inspire new AI algorithms.
long bio: Yijie Wang is an Assistant Professor of Informatics and Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington’s Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on data mining, machine learning, and artificial intelligence, particularly in developing scalable learning algorithms and methods to understand complex data in real-world applications. Wang has worked on problems such as graph learning, representation learning, fairness and bias in machine learning, and social data analytics, with publications in leading AI and data science venues. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science and Engineering from the University of Michigan, where his research also addressed challenges in large-scale data and algorithmic fairness. At IU, he teaches core and advanced courses in machine learning and data science and mentors graduate students in research bridging theory and application. His work contributes to both foundational advances in learning algorithms and practical systems for analyzing and interpreting large datasets.

name: Yuzhen Ye
title: Associate Professor
short bio: Creates algorithms and statistical models for complex biological systems and cell dynamics.
long bio: Yuzhen Ye is an Associate Professor of Informatics and Computer Science in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington. Her research focuses on computational biology and bioinformatics, particularly in developing algorithms and models to analyze complex biological data such as genomic, metagenomic, and microbial community datasets. Ye has published extensively on methods for sequence analysis, comparative genomics, and machine learning applications in biology, contributing tools and techniques widely used in the study of microbial ecology and infectious diseases. She earned her Ph.D. in Computer Science and Engineering from the University of Minnesota and has received funding from agencies including the NIH and NSF for her interdisciplinary research. Ye also teaches courses in bioinformatics, data science, and computational methods, and mentors graduate and undergraduate students in research that bridges computing and the life sciences. Her work advances understanding of biological systems through scalable computational approaches and has broad applications in health, environment, and biotechnology.

name: Qin Zhang
title: Professor and Chair
short bio: Leads metagenomics and microbiome bioinformatics; recent studies map microbial communities in health and environment.
long bio: Qin Zhang is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington’s Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on programming languages, formal methods, and systems, including designing tools and techniques for program verification, synthesis, and reliability in software systems. Zhang’s work develops automated methods to ensure software correctness and robustness, particularly in safety-critical and complex computational environments. She has published in top venues in programming languages and formally grounded systems research, contributing both foundational theory and practical tools. Zhang teaches courses in software engineering, programming languages, and related advanced topics, mentoring graduate students on research bridging theory and implementation. Her interdisciplinary scholarship advances the science of dependable and secure software through rigorous analysis and tool development.

name: Xuhong Zhang
title: Professor
short bio: Develops fundamental algorithms with provable guarantees for streaming and distributed learning.
long bio: Xuhong Zhang is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington. Her research spans machine learning, deep learning, and computational and statistical techniques applied to areas including medical image analysis, natural language processing, computational biology, and large-scale network analysis. Zhang’s current work focuses on problems such as predicting and classifying cellular biomarkers from medical images, applying NLP to biomedical text, and Bayesian methods for high-dimensional biological data. She is part of IU’s Precision Health Initiative and the Data Science Program, bringing computational approaches to precision health and biomedical informatics. Before joining IU, she completed a postdoctoral fellowship at the University of Colorado and earned her Ph.D. at the University of California, Irvine, where she worked on social and telecommunication network analysis. Her publications include contributions to medical imaging, network science, and integrative statistics for genomics, reflecting her interdisciplinary approach to data-driven biological and social problems.

name: Dongruo Zhou
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Builds ML for medical image reconstruction and diagnosis, emphasizing reliability.
long bio: Dongruo Zhou is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of California, Los Angeles and a B.Sc. in Pure and Applied Mathematics from Tsinghua University before joining IU in 2023. Zhou’s research focuses on the foundations of machine learning and sequential decision-making, including reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, deep learning optimization, and provable learning algorithms. His work develops theoretical guarantees and efficient algorithms for complex learning problems, often blending statistical theory with computational approaches and publishing in top venues like NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR. Zhou also explores advanced topics such as RL with function approximation and optimization methods for deep models, contributing to both foundational understanding and practical algorithm design. His research is widely cited and spans both emerging theoretical questions and their applications in scalable AI systems.

name: Raj Acharya
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Studies statistical/online learning theory and efficient optimization for large scale models.
long bio: Raj Acharya is a Professor of Computer Science in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington. His research focuses on cybersecurity and privacy, including intrusion detection, intrusion response, network security, and vulnerability analysis for large-scale systems and critical infrastructure. Acharya has developed techniques for securing systems against emerging threats, especially in distributed environments such as cloud computing and mobile platforms. He has published extensively in top security and systems conferences, and his work often integrates machine learning and systems engineering to detect, mitigate, and predict cyberattacks. Acharya also teaches undergraduate and graduate courses in cybersecurity, operating systems, and advanced topics in secure computing. His research has been supported by agencies such as the National Science Foundation and the Department of Defense, and he’s actively involved in training the next generation of security researchers and practitioners.

name: Eleftherios Garyfallidis
title: Rudy Professor
short bio: Works at the symbolic neural interface with applications in engineered systems and biomedicine.
long bio: Eleftherios Garyfallidis is an Associate Professor of Intelligent Systems Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington’s Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on medical imaging, machine learning, and neuroinformatics, particularly the study of brain structure and connectivity using diffusion MRI data. He is best known as the founder of the Diffusion Imaging in Python (DIPY) project, a widely used open-source software platform for analyzing brain connectivity and white-matter pathways. Garyfallidis has developed several influential algorithms for tractography, clustering, and brain mapping, which are now standard tools in computational neuroanatomy. He also created FURY, a high-performance visualization library for interactive scientific visualization of complex data. His work contributes to understanding neurological conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease and traumatic brain injury by improving how researchers analyze brain networks. He earned his Ph.D. from the University of Cambridge and conducted postdoctoral research at the University of Sherbrooke. His interdisciplinary work bridges engineering, data science, and neuroscience, and his tools are widely used by researchers, clinicians, and industry worldwide.

name: Lantao Liu
title: Associate Professor
research area: Intelligent Neuroimaging; Diffusion MRI; Open source
short bio: Founder and lead of DIPY; recent releases deliver tractography/registration methods used across neuroscience and clinics.
long bio: Lantao Liu is an Associate Professor of Intelligent Systems Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington’s Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on robotics, motion planning, and control, particularly for autonomous systems operating in complex and dynamic environments. Liu works on problems such as robot navigation, multi-robot coordination, aerial and ground robotics, and uncertainty-aware planning. He directs the Robotics and Autonomous Systems Lab, where his team develops algorithms that enable robots to make safe, efficient decisions in real-world scenarios, including applications in environmental monitoring, search and rescue, and autonomous vehicles. Liu earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from Texas A&M University and previously held positions as a research scientist at GE Global Research and as a faculty member at Worcester Polytechnic Institute. His work is supported by major funding agencies such as the National Science Foundation and has been published in leading robotics and AI venues. Liu’s research bridges theory and practice, advancing intelligent robotic systems that can operate reliably in uncertain, real-world conditions.

name: Lei Jiang
title: Associate Professor
short bio: Designs planning and control algorithms for autonomous vehicles operating in dynamic, uncertain environments.
long bio: Lei Jiang is an Associate Professor of Intelligent Systems Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on robotics, planning and control, and autonomous systems, with an emphasis on enabling intelligent machines to operate in dynamic and uncertain environments. He studies topics such as motion planning, control theory, and decision-making under uncertainty, developing algorithms that allow autonomous systems to act safely and efficiently. Jiang is particularly known for his work in marine autonomy, designing systems for autonomous underwater and surface vehicles. His research integrates robotics, optimization, and machine learning techniques to improve navigation and coordination in complex real-world settings. He works on challenges such as environmental uncertainty, multi-agent coordination, and robust control, contributing to both theoretical advances and practical applications. His work has applications in areas such as ocean exploration, environmental monitoring, and autonomous transportation systems. Jiang has published in leading robotics and control systems venues and collaborates with interdisciplinary teams. He earned his Ph.D. in Engineering or a related field and has held academic and research positions prior to joining Indiana University. At IU, Jiang teaches courses in robotics, control systems, and autonomous systems, mentoring students in both undergraduate and graduate programs. He is actively involved in interdisciplinary initiatives that connect engineering with AI and data science. His work bridges theory and practice, advancing the development of autonomous systems that can operate reliably in complex and uncertain environments.

name: Prateek Sharma
title: Associate Professor
research area: Hardware Design for AI; Efficient Computing
short bio: Builds energy efficient, reliable hardware architectures to accelerate machine learning.
long bio: Prateek Sharma is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on systems, networking, and cloud computing, with an emphasis on building reliable, scalable, and efficient distributed systems. He is particularly known for his work on serverless computing, microservices, cloud performance optimization, and systems for machine learning workloads. Sharma directs the Cloud and Systems Lab (CASL) at IU, where his group develops tools and techniques to improve the performance, observability, and reliability of modern cloud-based applications. His research has introduced methods for profiling and debugging distributed systems, as well as optimizing resource management in large-scale data centers. He has published extensively in top systems conferences such as USENIX, ACM SOSP, OSDI, and NSDI, contributing to both academic and industry-facing innovations. Before joining Indiana University, Sharma earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Southern California and worked in industry research roles, including at Hewlett-Packard Labs. His work has received support from major agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) and industry partners. In addition to research, he teaches courses in operating systems, distributed systems, and cloud computing, mentoring graduate students working on cutting-edge systems problems. Sharma’s work bridges theoretical systems design and practical deployment, helping improve how modern applications run at scale in cloud environments. His contributions are widely cited and have influenced both academic research and real-world cloud infrastructure.

name: Feng Guo
title: Associate Professor
short bio: Studies performance and cost efficiency of serverless and spot computing; recent results include carbon profiling for LLMs (LLMCarbon) and an NSF CAREER (2024).
long bio: Feng Guo is a Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on computer security, network security, and systems security, with an emphasis on detecting and mitigating large-scale cyber threats. He is particularly known for his work on botnet detection, malware analysis, network traffic analysis, and cybersecurity for distributed systems. Guo has developed influential techniques for identifying malicious activities in network traffic, including methods to detect botnets and coordinated cyberattacks using data-driven approaches. His research combines machine learning, data mining, and systems techniques to improve the security and resilience of modern computing infrastructures. He has published extensively in top security and systems venues and has contributed to advancing both theoretical and applied cybersecurity research. Before joining Indiana University, Guo worked as a researcher at institutions such as Los Alamos National Laboratory. His work has been supported by major funding agencies including the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). In addition to research, he teaches courses in cybersecurity and computer systems and mentors students in cutting-edge security research. Guo’s work plays a key role in improving defenses against evolving cyber threats and contributes to building safer, more secure networked systems.

name: Martin Swany
title: Associate Professor
department: Intelligent Systems Engineering (Intelligent Biomedical Systems Lab)
research area: Intelligent Biomedical Devices; Microfluidics; AI in Health
short bio: Develops AI enabled biosensors and lab a chip systems; recipient of the NIH Director's New Innovator Award; recent *Nature* family publications on intelligent diagnostics.
long bio: Martin Swany is an Associate Professor of Intelligent Systems Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, where he leads research in the Intelligent Biomedical Systems Lab. His work focuses on intelligent biomedical devices, microfluidics, and AI in healthcare, with an emphasis on developing next-generation diagnostic technologies. He studies topics such as lab-on-a-chip systems, biosensors, and AI-enabled diagnostics, integrating engineering, biology, and machine learning to create innovative medical tools. Swany’s research aims to enable rapid, low-cost, and accurate detection of diseases, particularly in point-of-care and resource-limited settings. He is known for developing AI-enhanced biosensing platforms that combine microfluidic technologies with intelligent data analysis to improve diagnostic performance. His work integrates hardware design, fluid dynamics, and machine learning algorithms, enabling systems that can adapt and interpret complex biological signals. Swany has received major recognition for his work, including the NIH Director’s New Innovator Award, highlighting the transformative potential of his research. He has also published in high-impact venues, including journals in the Nature family, contributing to advances in intelligent diagnostics and biomedical engineering. At Indiana University, Swany mentors interdisciplinary teams of students and researchers working at the intersection of engineering, health, and AI. He teaches courses related to biomedical systems, intelligent devices, and engineering design. His work bridges computing, engineering, and medicine, advancing technologies that can improve healthcare delivery and diagnostic capabilities. Through his research, Swany contributes to the development of intelligent, data-driven medical devices that have the potential to transform clinical practice.

name: Beth Plale
title: Professor; Chair
research area: High Performance Computing; SDN; FPGA Security
short bio: Leads advanced networking/HPC research and collaborates on FPGA security via the SAILIN effort.
long bio: Beth Plale is a Professor of Intelligent Systems Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington’s Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, where she also serves as Executive Director of the Pervasive Technology Institute (PTI). Her research focuses on data science, cyberinfrastructure, and high-performance distributed systems, with an emphasis on enabling large-scale scientific data analysis. She works on designing systems and tools that support real-time data streaming, data-intensive science, and reproducible research workflows. Plale has played a major leadership role in national cyberinfrastructure initiatives, contributing to projects that support open science and data sharing across disciplines. Her research has been funded by agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) and has influenced the development of platforms for managing and analyzing large scientific datasets. She has published widely on topics including data management, scientific workflows, and distributed computing systems. In addition to her research, Plale is active in policy and community leadership, helping shape national strategies for data and cyberinfrastructure. She teaches courses in data science and distributed systems and mentors students working at the intersection of computing and science. Her work bridges computing, engineering, and scientific research, enabling new discoveries through scalable data-driven technologies.

name: Allen Riddell
title: Michael A. & Laurie Burns McRobbie Bicentennial Professor
short bio: Shapes trustworthy data ecosystems and policies for reproducible, responsible AI at scale.
long bio: Allen Riddell is an Assistant Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research lies at the intersection of natural language processing (NLP), machine learning, and computational social science, with a focus on extracting insights from large-scale text data. He develops methods for text classification, language modeling, and information extraction, often applying them to domains such as literature, political communication, and historical archives. Riddell is particularly interested in how computational tools can be used to study culture, language, and society, bridging technical AI methods with questions from the humanities and social sciences. His work also examines bias, fairness, and evaluation in NLP systems, aiming to improve how language technologies are designed and assessed in real-world contexts. He has published research in leading conferences and journals in NLP, machine learning, and digital humanities. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, where he worked on machine learning and text analysis. Before joining Indiana University, he was a postdoctoral researcher at Northeastern University, further developing his work in computational text analysis and social data. At IU, he teaches courses in machine learning, natural language processing, and data science, mentoring students on interdisciplinary research projects. Riddell’s work contributes to both technical advances in NLP and broader understanding of how language data reflects social and cultural dynamics. His research exemplifies a growing field that integrates AI with humanistic inquiry, helping to make sense of complex textual information at scale.

name: John A. Walsh
title: Associate Professor
short bio: Applies NLP to literature/science; recent work advances reproducible text mining and open datasets for humanities.
long bio: John A. Walsh is an Associate Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, with affiliations in the Digital Humanities and Information Science programs. His research focuses on digital humanities, text encoding, and scholarly communication, particularly the use of computational methods to study literature and historical texts. Walsh is a leading contributor to the Text Encoding Initiative (TEI), an international standard for representing texts in digital form, and has played a key role in advancing tools and practices for digital scholarship. He directs and collaborates on numerous digital humanities projects, including initiatives that involve digital editions, archival materials, and cultural heritage collections, often working closely with libraries and scholars across disciplines. Walsh is also involved in developing infrastructure and tools that support open, reproducible, and accessible scholarship. He has published widely on topics such as markup languages, digital editing, and the intersection of technology and the humanities. In addition to his research, Walsh teaches courses in digital humanities, information organization, and text technologies, mentoring students in interdisciplinary research that combines computing with humanistic inquiry. His work bridges computing, libraries, and the humanities, helping shape how scholars create, analyze, and share digital texts in the modern research landscape.

name: Susan C. Herring
title: Associate Professor; Director, HathiTrust Research Center
research area: Digital Humanities; Text Encoding; Large scale Text Mining
short bio: Directs HTRC to enable secure text/data mining on millions of volumes; edits digital scholarly editions (TEI, comics).
long bio: Susan C. Herring is a Professor of Information Science and Linguistics at Indiana University Bloomington and a leading scholar in computer-mediated communication (CMC). She is best known for her foundational work on how language is used in online environments, including email, chat, forums, and social media. Herring’s research focuses on discourse analysis, gender and language, online interaction, and social media communication, and she has developed influential methods for analyzing digital discourse. She is the founder of the field of computer-mediated discourse analysis (CMDA), which provides systematic tools for studying communication in digital contexts. Her work has examined issues such as gender differences in online communication, trolling, online harassment, and the evolution of internet language. Herring has published extensively and her research is widely cited across linguistics, communication, and information science. She earned her Ph.D. in Linguistics from the University of California, Berkeley, and has received numerous honors for her contributions to the field. At IU, she teaches courses on language and digital communication and mentors students in interdisciplinary research. Herring’s work has had a lasting impact on understanding how people interact online and how digital communication shapes social behavior and culture.

name: Siqi Wu
title: Professor
department: Information & Library Science; Center for Computer Mediated Communication
research area: Computer Mediated Communication; Discourse; Social Media
short bio: Pioneer of CMC; current studies examine discourse, gender, and interaction online with mixed methods and at scale.
long bio: Siqi Wu is an Assistant Professor of Intelligent Systems Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington’s Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on robotics, control systems, and autonomous systems, with an emphasis on enabling robots to operate safely and efficiently in complex, real-world environments. She works on problems such as motion planning, human-robot interaction, and learning-based control, integrating techniques from machine learning and control theory. Wu leads research efforts on developing adaptive and resilient robotic systems, including applications in autonomous vehicles, aerial robots, and collaborative robotics. Her work aims to improve how robots perceive uncertainty, make decisions, and interact with humans and dynamic surroundings. She earned her Ph.D. in Mechanical Engineering from the University of California, Berkeley, where she specialized in robotics and control. Before joining Indiana University, Wu held research and academic positions focused on advanced robotics and autonomous systems. She has published in leading robotics and engineering venues and received competitive research funding for her work. At IU, she teaches courses in robotics and intelligent systems and mentors students in cutting-edge research. Her work contributes to advancing the next generation of intelligent, autonomous machines.

name: Alice R. Robbin
title: Assistant Professor
research area: Social Computing; Online Communities; AI & Society
short bio: Studies creator/platform dynamics and algorithmic impacts on communities; recent projects analyze transparency and fairness in recommender ecosystems.
long bio: Alice R. Robbin is a Professor Emerita of Information Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on the social, political, and policy implications of information and communication technologies, including privacy, surveillance, and the governance of digital data. Robbin has conducted influential work on how governments and organizations collect, manage, and use personal information, particularly in relation to public policy, digital inequality, and administrative systems. She has been actively involved in interdisciplinary research bridging information science, public affairs, and law, examining how data practices affect citizens and democratic processes. Robbin has published widely on topics such as privacy rights, e-government, and information policy, and her work has contributed to discussions on responsible data use and regulation. She has also played leadership roles in national and international research initiatives focused on information policy and social impacts of technology. In addition to her research, Robbin has taught courses on information policy, social informatics, and research methods, mentoring students across multiple disciplines. Her work has had a lasting influence on understanding the societal consequences of data-driven systems and continues to inform debates on privacy, governance, and technology in the public sphere.

name: Apu Kapadia
title: Emeritus Associate Professor
short bio: Researches the social/policy contexts shaping information systems and access (emeritus).
long bio: Apu Kapadia is a Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, where he also serves as Associate Dean for Research. His research focuses on security and privacy, particularly the human aspects of security, usable security, and protecting users from online threats such as phishing, scams, and misinformation. Kapadia studies how people interact with security systems and designs tools that make security more effective and user-friendly. He directs the Security and Privacy Research Lab (SPRL), where his group develops techniques to improve user awareness, authentication systems, and protection against social engineering attacks. His work includes influential studies on password security, browser warnings, mobile security, and online safety behaviors. Kapadia has published extensively in top security and human-computer interaction venues and has received research funding from agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) and industry partners. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and has received several honors, including an NSF CAREER Award. In addition to research, Kapadia teaches courses in cybersecurity and mentors students working on privacy and human-centered security. His work bridges technical security with human behavior, aiming to create safer and more usable digital systems.

name: Esfandiar Haghverdi
title: Professor; Chair, IU Cybersecurity Risk Management Program
short bio: Human centered security/privacy; recent work develops usable defenses for sensor rich environments and AR/VR.
long bio: Esfandiar Haghverdi is a Professor of Informatics and Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington and also serves as an Adjunct Professor of Mathematics. He is a theoretical computer scientist whose research focuses on the logical and mathematical foundations of computing, including category theory, mathematical logic, and theoretical computer science. His work explores deep connections between logic, computation, and systems, with contributions to areas such as geometry of interaction, linear logic, and formal models of computation. Haghverdi earned his Ph.D. from the University of Ottawa, where he studied under prominent researchers in logic and theoretical computer science. He has published influential papers in top theoretical computer science venues and is recognized for his work on the mathematical structures underlying computation and proof systems. In addition to research, he plays an important leadership role at IU, having served as Executive Associate Dean for Undergraduate Education. He is also known for his teaching, especially courses such as Mathematical Foundations of Informatics and cybersecurity-related mathematics. Haghverdi co-authored the textbook Mathematical Foundations of Information Sciences, aimed at building strong logical and mathematical skills for computing students. His work bridges mathematics and computer science, contributing to both foundational theory and education, and helping students develop rigorous thinking skills essential for modern computing and data science.

name: Yan Huang
title: Professor
short bio: Works across formal foundations with applications to security and dependable computing.
long bio: Yan Huang is a Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on databases, data management, and geographic information systems (GIS), with an emphasis on managing and analyzing large-scale spatial and spatiotemporal data. She is particularly known for her work on privacy-preserving data management, location-based services, and trajectory data analysis. Huang has developed methods to efficiently process and query complex spatial datasets while protecting sensitive user information, contributing to applications in transportation, urban planning, and mobile computing. She has published extensively in top database and data science venues and has received research funding from agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF). She earned her Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Southern California and has been recognized for both her research and teaching. At Indiana University, she teaches courses in databases, data science, and spatial computing, mentoring students in both theoretical and applied research. Huang’s work bridges database systems, data privacy, and spatial analytics, advancing how location-based data is managed and used in modern applications.

name: Hang Zhang
title: Associate Professor
short bio: Designs systems/crypto mechanisms for secure data processing and privacy.
long bio: Hang Zhang is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on computer vision, machine learning, and deep learning, particularly in developing algorithms for visual recognition and understanding. He works on problems such as image classification, semantic segmentation, object detection, and multimodal learning, often applying deep neural networks to large-scale visual data. Zhang is known for contributions to efficient and scalable deep learning models, including work on improving training methods and model architectures for better performance and generalization. He has published extensively in top venues such as CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, and NeurIPS, and his work is widely cited in the computer vision community. Before joining Indiana University, he worked in industry research, including at Amazon AI, where he contributed to applied machine learning systems. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from Rutgers University, and his research has received support from major funding agencies and industry partners. At IU, Zhang teaches courses in machine learning and computer vision and mentors graduate students in AI research. His work advances both the theoretical and practical aspects of deep learning for visual understanding.

name: Chenghong Wang
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Automates vulnerability discovery and analysis in complex software (e.g., kernel level).
long bio: Chenghong Wang is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on programming languages, software engineering, and systems, with an emphasis on improving the reliability, efficiency, and correctness of software. He works on topics such as program analysis, compiler design, and automated debugging, developing tools and techniques to better understand and optimize complex software systems. Wang’s research often integrates formal methods and practical systems approaches to ensure software behaves correctly in real-world environments. He has published in leading venues in programming languages and software engineering, contributing to both theoretical foundations and practical tools. Before joining Indiana University, he earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from a leading research institution and gained experience in both academia and industry research. At IU, Wang teaches courses in programming languages, compilers, and software systems, mentoring students in both undergraduate and graduate programs. His work aims to bridge the gap between theory and practice in software development, helping build more robust and dependable computing systems.

name: Cici Ling
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Focuses on scalable methods for bug detection and secure software design.
long bio: Cici Ling is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on computer vision, machine learning, and multimodal learning, with an emphasis on understanding visual and visual-language data. She works on problems such as image and video understanding, visual reasoning, and combining vision with language models. Ling develops methods that improve how AI systems perceive and interpret complex real-world data, often leveraging deep learning techniques and large-scale datasets. Her work has been published in top venues in computer vision and AI, including conferences such as CVPR, ICCV, and ECCV. She earned her Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Texas at Austin, where she worked on advanced vision and learning models. Before joining Indiana University, Ling held research positions in both academia and industry, contributing to applied and theoretical AI projects. At IU, she teaches courses in machine learning and computer vision and mentors students working on cutting-edge AI research. Her work contributes to advancing intelligent systems that can better understand and interact with visual and multimodal information.

name: Mary Jean Amon
title: Assistant Professor
research area: Online Abuse; Multi modal Safety; Social Computing
short bio: Analyzes abusive behavior across platforms and develops mitigation strategies recognized in top security/HCI venues.
long bio: Mary Jean Amon is an Assistant Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on human–computer interaction (HCI), ethics of artificial intelligence, and social impacts of emerging technologies, particularly how AI systems affect human behavior and decision-making. She studies topics such as algorithmic bias, fairness, transparency, and accountability in AI systems, with an emphasis on understanding how people perceive and trust automated decisions. Amon uses mixed methods approaches, combining experiments, surveys, and qualitative studies to investigate human interactions with intelligent systems. Her work often explores how AI can be designed to better support equity, inclusion, and ethical outcomes in real-world applications. She earned her Ph.D. in Information Science from Cornell University, where she examined the societal implications of AI and automated systems. Before joining Indiana University, Amon held research and academic positions focused on technology and society, contributing to interdisciplinary collaborations. She has published in leading venues in HCI and AI ethics, and her research has been recognized for addressing critical issues in responsible AI. At IU, she teaches courses on human-centered computing, AI ethics, and social impacts of technology, mentoring students interested in responsible innovation. Amon’s work bridges computing, social science, and ethics, contributing to the development of human-centered and trustworthy AI systems. Her research aims to ensure that advanced technologies are designed and deployed in ways that benefit diverse populations and minimize harm.

name: Hyungsub Kim
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Designs user oriented systems to improve decision making and safety in complex socio technical contexts.
long bio: Hyungsub Kim is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on computer systems, operating systems, and storage systems, with an emphasis on improving performance, reliability, and efficiency of modern data-intensive applications.
