He works on problems related to non-volatile memory, file systems, distributed storage, and cloud infrastructure, designing systems that can better support emerging hardware and large-scale workloads. Kim’s research explores how to optimize data access and storage in environments such as data centers and high-performance computing systems. He has developed techniques to enhance storage performance, consistency, and fault tolerance, contributing to both theoretical understanding and practical system design. His work has been published in top systems conferences such as USENIX, FAST, and SOSP, and is widely recognized in the systems research community. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Texas at Austin, where he specialized in systems and storage technologies. Before joining Indiana University, he held research and academic positions contributing to advancements in storage and systems design. At IU, Kim teaches courses in operating systems and computer systems and mentors students working on cutting-edge systems research. His work bridges hardware and software systems, helping improve how data is stored, accessed, and managed in modern computing environments.

name: Jacob G. Foster
title: Assistant Professor
research area: System Security; Formal Methods; Cyber physical Systems
short bio: Secures robotic vehicles and embedded systems via formal analysis and patch verification.
long bio: Jacob G. Foster is a Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, with affiliations in Sociology and Cognitive Science. His research focuses on computational social science, cultural evolution, and the science of science, using network analysis and statistical models to study how ideas, beliefs, and knowledge systems change over time. He investigates topics such as scientific innovation, knowledge diffusion, interdisciplinarity, and cultural dynamics, often analyzing large-scale datasets of publications and social systems. Foster has developed influential methods for modeling how scientific fields emerge, grow, and interact, contributing to a deeper understanding of how knowledge is produced and organized. His work bridges sociology, data science, and informatics, combining theoretical frameworks with empirical data analysis. He has published widely in leading journals and his research has been supported by agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF). He earned his Ph.D. in Sociology from Princeton University and previously held academic positions at other major research institutions before joining Indiana University. At IU, Foster teaches courses on computational social science, networks, and data analysis, mentoring students across disciplines. His interdisciplinary work provides insights into the structure and evolution of knowledge systems, helping explain how science and culture develop in complex, data-rich environments.

name: Michael McRobbie
title: Professor
short bio: Studies principles of diverse intelligences and the social production of ideas; directs DI Summer Institute and the Center for Possible Minds.
long bio: Michael McRobbie is a Professor of Informatics and Cognitive Science at Indiana University Bloomington and a prominent scholar in cognitive AI, natural language processing, and collective intelligence. His research focuses on understanding the principles of diverse intelligences, including how human, artificial, and collective systems generate knowledge and ideas. He studies topics such as language understanding, reasoning, and the social production of ideas, exploring how intelligence emerges across individuals and groups. McRobbie’s work integrates AI, cognitive science, and philosophy, contributing to foundational questions about intelligence and knowledge. He is actively involved in interdisciplinary initiatives, including directing the Digital Intelligence (DI) Summer Institute, which brings together scholars to study the future of intelligence in society. He also leads the Center for Possible Minds, an initiative that explores the ethical, social, and technical implications of advanced AI systems. His research emphasizes the importance of collaborative and distributed intelligence, examining how ideas are produced through interaction and communication. He has published and contributed to discussions on AI, cognition, and the future of intelligent systems. At Indiana University, McRobbie teaches courses related to AI, cognitive science, and digital intelligence, mentoring students in interdisciplinary research. He plays a key role in advancing IU’s leadership in AI and society research initiatives. His work bridges computing, philosophy, and social science, advancing understanding of how intelligence operates across human and artificial systems. Through his leadership and scholarship, McRobbie contributes to shaping the future of AI, collective intelligence, and knowledge creation.

name: David B. Leake
title: University Chancellor & University Professor
short bio: Leads initiatives at the intersection of AI systems and research cyberinfrastructure.
long bio: David B. Leake is a Professor of Informatics and Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, where he also serves as Associate Dean for Research. His research focuses on artificial intelligence, particularly case-based reasoning, knowledge management, and intelligent decision-support systems. He studies how systems can use past experiences to solve new problems, with applications in areas such as law, healthcare, engineering design, and sustainability. Leake has made foundational contributions to case-based reasoning, including methods for retrieving, adapting, and explaining prior cases to support decision making. His work also explores human-AI collaboration, organizational learning, and how AI systems can better support human expertise. He has published extensively in leading AI journals and conferences and has edited influential volumes in the field. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from Yale University and has received research funding from agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the Department of Defense. In addition to his research, Leake teaches courses in artificial intelligence and leads initiatives to expand AI research and education at Indiana University. Leake’s work bridges foundational AI research with practical applications, contributing to the development of intelligent systems that learn from experience and support complex decision-making processes.

name: Selma Å abanoviÄ‡
title: Professor
short bio: Case based reasoning and explanation in intelligent systems.
long bio: Selma Šabanović is an Associate Professor of Informatics and Cognitive Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on human–robot interaction (HRI), social robotics, and the social, cultural, and ethical implications of robotics and AI systems. She studies how people interact with robots in real-world settings and how social context influences the design, acceptance, and impact of robotic technologies. Šabanović directs the R-House (Robotics for Humanity) Lab, where her team designs and evaluates socially assistive robots for applications such as eldercare, education, and healthcare. Her work emphasizes human-centered and participatory design, ensuring that robotic systems are inclusive, culturally sensitive, and responsive to users’ needs. She has conducted field studies in diverse environments, including homes, schools, and care facilities, to understand how robots can support human well-being. She earned her Ph.D. in Science and Technology Studies from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and has received funding from agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF). Her research has been widely published in leading HRI and HCI venues and has contributed to shaping the interdisciplinary field of social robotics. At IU, she teaches courses on human–robot interaction, ethics of AI, and design of interactive systems. Šabanović’s work bridges engineering, social science, and design, advancing the development of robotic systems that are socially aware, ethical, and beneficial to diverse communities.

name: Xiaojing Liao
title: Professor; Associate Dean for Faculty Affairs
research area: Human Robot Interaction; Social Robotics; STS
short bio: Combines HRI with social studies of computing to design and evaluate socially/ culturally situated robots; recent projects explore long term companionship, participatory design with older adults, and responsible stewardship of robotic systems.
long bio: Xiaojing Liao is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on computer security, privacy, and applied cryptography, with an emphasis on protecting systems and users from emerging cyber threats. She studies problems such as malware analysis, network security, and vulnerabilities in large-scale systems, developing techniques to detect and mitigate attacks. Liao’s work often combines systems research with data-driven methods, including machine learning approaches for identifying malicious behavior in software and network traffic. She has contributed to understanding real-world security threats and improving defenses against attacks targeting both infrastructure and end users. Her research has been published in top security venues such as IEEE S&P, USENIX Security, and CCS, and is widely cited in the cybersecurity community. She earned her Ph.D. in Computer Science from the Georgia Institute of Technology, where she specialized in systems and security research. Before joining Indiana University, she held research positions focused on cybersecurity and system analysis. At IU, Liao teaches courses in computer security and mentors students in cutting-edge research on privacy and system protection. Her work advances the development of secure and trustworthy computing systems, addressing critical challenges in modern cybersecurity.

name: Katy Börner
title: Associate Professor
short bio: Measures adversarial behaviors and platform abuse at Internet scale; recent work detects coordinated malicious activity and builds robust defenses.
long bio: Katy Börner is a Distinguished Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, and a leading scholar in network science, data visualization, and the science of science. She is the founding director of the Cyberinfrastructure for Network Science Center (CNS) and a core faculty member of the IU Network Science Institute. Her research focuses on mapping and modeling complex networks, including scientific knowledge, collaboration networks, and information systems, often using advanced visualization techniques. Börner is widely known for her work in scientific visualization and knowledge mapping, helping researchers understand the structure and evolution of science and innovation. She is the author of influential books such as Atlas of Science: Visualizing What We Know and Atlas of Forecasts, which present large-scale visualizations of scientific and societal systems. Her work has been supported by major agencies including the National Science Foundation (NSF) and has contributed to tools used by researchers, policymakers, and educators. She earned her Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Kaiserslautern in Germany and has received numerous honors for her contributions, including being named a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS). At IU, she teaches courses on data visualization and network science and mentors students across disciplines. Börner’s work bridges computing, information science, and design, advancing how complex data is analyzed and communicated through visual representations.

name: David J. Crandall
title: Distinguished Professor; Director, Cyberinfrastructure for Network Science Center
department: Intelligent Systems Engineering & Information and Library Science (CNS)
research area: Data Visualization; Science Mapping; Human Reference Atlas
short bio: Crandall leads vision and multimodal ML research spanning recognition, 3D/egocentric perception (e.g., Ego4D), and HRI collaborations. He held leadership roles at CVPR/AAAI and received the Sonneborn Award, with sustained outputs across CVPR/ICCV/CHI.
long bio: David J. Crandall is a Professor of Computer Science and Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on computer vision, machine learning, and artificial intelligence, with an emphasis on understanding visual data and its interaction with social systems. He works on problems such as image and video analysis, scene understanding, deep learning, and multimodal data analysis, often combining visual data with social or contextual information. Crandall is known for contributions to large-scale visual recognition systems and for exploring how AI systems can interpret complex, real-world imagery. His work also examines the societal and ethical implications of AI, including issues related to bias, privacy, and the use of machine learning in social contexts. He has published extensively in top venues such as CVPR, ICCV, and NeurIPS, and his research is widely cited in both computer vision and AI communities. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from Cornell University and has received research funding from agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) and DARPA. At Indiana University, he teaches courses in computer vision, machine learning, and artificial intelligence, mentoring students across undergraduate and graduate programs. Crandall’s work bridges technical innovation with real-world applications, advancing both the capabilities of visual AI systems and understanding of their broader societal impact.

name: Randall D. Beer
title: Luddy Professor; Director, Luddy AI Center; Director, Center for Machine Learning
research area: Computer Vision; Multimodal ML; Egocentric Perception
long bio: Randall D. Beer is a Distinguished Professor of Informatics and Cognitive Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, and a leading researcher in cognitive science, artificial intelligence, and dynamical systems. His research focuses on the nature of intelligence and adaptive behavior, particularly how cognition emerges from the interaction of brain, body, and environment. He studies topics such as neural dynamics, embodied cognition, and evolutionary robotics, using computational models to explore fundamental principles of intelligence. Beer is widely known for advancing dynamical systems approaches to cognition, challenging traditional symbolic models and emphasizing continuous, real-time processes. His work often involves building and analyzing minimal agent-based models to understand perception, action, and decision-making in both biological and artificial systems. He has contributed significantly to fields such as theoretical neuroscience, cognitive modeling, and artificial life, with widely cited publications. Beer earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Texas at Austin and has held faculty positions at Case Western Reserve University before joining Indiana University. His research has been supported by agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF). At Indiana University, Beer teaches courses in cognitive science, complex systems, and computational modeling, mentoring students across disciplines. He is actively involved in interdisciplinary collaborations that connect computing, psychology, and neuroscience. His work bridges theory and experiment, advancing understanding of how intelligence arises in natural and artificial systems. Through his research, Beer contributes to foundational questions about learning, behavior, and the dynamics of cognition.

name: Damir Cavar
title: Professor
short bio: Cavar works on NLP and computational linguistics, including parsing and corpus‑driven modeling. He participates in AI Center NLP initiatives and cross‑department collaborations.
long bio: Damir Cavar is a Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on computational linguistics, natural language processing (NLP), and language technologies, with an emphasis on multilingual and low-resource languages. He works on problems such as language modeling, information extraction, speech and text processing, and linguistic annotation, often combining computational methods with linguistic theory. Cavar has contributed to the development of tools and resources for language analysis and digital humanities, including work on corpora, lexicons, and language processing systems. His research also explores AI applications in language, including large language models and language understanding systems. He has published widely in computational linguistics and has been involved in numerous international collaborations. He earned his Ph.D. in Linguistics from the University of Potsdam in Germany and has held academic positions in Europe and the United States before joining Indiana University. At IU, he teaches courses in NLP, computational linguistics, and data science, mentoring students in interdisciplinary language and AI research. Cavar’s work bridges linguistics and computer science, advancing technologies that enable machines to understand and process human language across diverse contexts.

name: Sandra Kübler
title: Associate Professor
short bio: Kübler’s work spans multilingual parsing and linguistic resources that power downstream NLP tasks. She engages with the AI Center’s language community and contributes to training datasets and toolchains.
long bio: Sandra Kübler is a Professor of Linguistics and Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington, with appointments in both the Department of Linguistics and the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on computational linguistics and natural language processing (NLP), particularly in areas such as syntactic parsing, corpus linguistics, and machine learning for language analysis. She is especially known for her work on parsing morphologically rich and low-resource languages, as well as developing annotated linguistic corpora. Kübler has made significant contributions to the development of treebanks and linguistic resources, which are essential for training and evaluating NLP systems. Her work combines linguistic theory with statistical and machine learning approaches, helping improve the accuracy and robustness of language technologies. She has published extensively in leading NLP and computational linguistics venues and has co-authored influential textbooks, including Dependency Parsing and Natural Language Processing in Action. She earned her Ph.D. in Computational Linguistics from the University of Tübingen in Germany and has held academic positions at institutions such as the University of Texas at Austin before joining Indiana University. At IU, Kübler teaches courses in NLP, corpus linguistics, and computational methods for language analysis, mentoring students across linguistics and computer science. Her work bridges linguistics and AI, advancing methods for understanding the structure and meaning of language across diverse linguistic contexts.

name: Byung‑Cheol Min
title: University Chancellor; President Emeritus; University Professor
short bio: Min develops field‑deployable autonomous systems and human‑robot teaming methods. His lab publishes in robotics/HRI venues and contributes to real‑world deployments.
long bio: Byung-Cheol (“B.C.”) Min is a Professor with joint appointments in Computer Science and Intelligent Systems Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington’s Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on robotics, human–robot interaction, and multi-robot systems, with an emphasis on enabling intelligent machines to collaborate with humans and operate in complex, real-world environments. He directs the SMART (Smart Machine and Robotics Technology) Lab, where his team develops methods in distributed robotics, reinforcement learning, and generative AI for robotic systems. Min’s work explores how groups of robots can coordinate, adapt, and learn in dynamic settings, including applications in autonomous systems, smart infrastructure, and disaster response. Before joining Indiana University, he was a faculty member at Purdue University from 2015 to 2025, where he also led the Applied AI Research Center. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer and Information Technology from Purdue University and completed postdoctoral research at Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute. He has published extensively in leading robotics and AI venues and has received major recognitions, including the NSF CAREER Award. In addition to research, Min teaches courses in robotics, AI, and intelligent systems, mentoring students in interdisciplinary projects. His work bridges machine learning, control, and robotics, advancing the development of collaborative and adaptive robotic systems.

name: Allen B. Riddell
title: Professor
short bio: Riddell applies NLP to literary history, cultural analytics, and style transfer problems at scale. His group’s work advances methods and datasets for humanities computation.
long bio: Allen B. Riddell is an Assistant Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research lies at the intersection of natural language processing (NLP), machine learning, and computational social science, with a focus on analyzing large-scale text data. He develops computational methods for text classification, language modeling, and information extraction, applying them to domains such as literature, political discourse, and historical texts. Riddell is particularly interested in how computational tools can be used to study culture, language, and society, bridging technical AI methods with questions from the humanities and social sciences. His work also examines bias, fairness, and evaluation in NLP systems, aiming to improve the design and assessment of language technologies in real-world settings. He has published in leading NLP and machine learning conferences and journals, contributing to both technical advances and interdisciplinary research. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Massachusetts Amherst and previously held a postdoctoral position at Northeastern University, where he further developed his work in computational text analysis. At Indiana University, he teaches courses in machine learning, natural language processing, and data science, mentoring students on projects that combine computing with social and cultural analysis.Riddell’s work exemplifies a growing field that integrates AI with the humanities, helping researchers understand complex textual data at scale. His research contributes to both improving NLP technologies and deepening insight into how language reflects social and cultural dynamics.

name: Sagar Samtani
title: Professor
department: Informatics (R‑House HRI Lab; Luddy AI Center)
short bio: Samtani’s program bridges threat intelligence, dark‑web analytics, and deep learning for cyber risk management. He is an AI Center affiliate researcher and co‑authors with Luddy faculty.
long bio: Sagar Samtani is an Associate Professor of Informatics and Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and data science, particularly in using AI to detect and analyze cyber threats. He works on problems such as cyber threat intelligence, dark web analytics, fraud detection, and security informatics, developing methods to identify malicious activities and emerging risks. Samtani directs the Cybersecurity and Intelligence Lab at IU, where his team builds systems to analyze large-scale data from online forums, marketplaces, and social platforms to uncover cybercrime patterns. His work often leverages machine learning, natural language processing, and network analysis to study threat actors and predict cyberattacks. He has published extensively in top cybersecurity and data science venues and has received funding from agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) and industry partners. He earned his Ph.D. in Management Information Systems from the University of Arizona, where he specialized in cybersecurity analytics. Before joining Indiana University, he held research positions and collaborated with government and industry organizations on security challenges. At IU, Samtani teaches courses in cybersecurity, data science, and analytics, mentoring students in applied and interdisciplinary research. His work bridges AI and cybersecurity, contributing to improved defenses against cybercrime and advancing the field of data-driven security intelligence.

name: Santo Fortunato
title: Associate Professor
department: Kelley School (Operations & Decision Technologies; AI Center affiliate)
short bio: Fortunato is known for seminal work on community detection and science of science and directs the Indiana University Network Science Institute (IUNI). He publishes across Physics Reports, PNAS, Nature Physics, and related venues.
long bio: Santo Fortunato is a Distinguished Professor of Informatics and Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington and a leading researcher in network science and complex systems. He is also affiliated with the IU Network Science Institute, where he contributes to interdisciplinary research on complex networks across domains. His work focuses on community detection, network modeling, and the science of science, studying how complex systems such as social networks and scientific fields evolve. Fortunato is widely recognized for his influential contributions to community detection algorithms, including work on methods to identify structure and clusters in large networks. His research also explores scientific impact, citation networks, and the dynamics of knowledge production, helping to understand how ideas spread and how scientific fields develop. He has published extensively in top journals such as Nature, Science, and PNAS, and his work is highly cited across physics, computer science, and social science. He earned his Ph.D. in Physics from the University of Leiden and previously held positions at institutions such as Aalto University before joining Indiana University. Fortunato has received numerous honors for his work, including recognition as a leading figure in network science and election as a fellow of major scientific societies. In addition to his research, he teaches courses on network science and complex systems and mentors students across disciplines. His work bridges physics, computer science, and social science, advancing the understanding of structure and dynamics in complex interconnected systems.

name: Filippo Radicchi
title: James H. Rudy Professor
research area: Network Science; Community Detection; Science of Science
short bio: Radicchi studies percolation, resilience, and higher‑order network dynamics with recent results in *Nature Communications*, *Nature Machine Intelligence*, and *Physical Review* venues. He also contributes ranking/embedding methods for complex systems.
long bio: Filippo Radicchi is a Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering and a core member of the IU Network Science Institute. His research focuses on network science, complex systems, and the science of science, with an emphasis on understanding the structure and dynamics of complex networks such as social, biological, and information systems. Radicchi is known for his work on community detection, network robustness, and multilayer networks, developing methods to analyze how networks evolve and respond to perturbations. He has also made important contributions to research evaluation and scientometrics, studying how to measure scientific impact and productivity using citation data and network-based metrics. His work often bridges theory and application, applying network models to real-world problems such as collaboration patterns and knowledge diffusion. He has published extensively in leading journals including Nature Communications, PNAS, and Physical Review Letters, and his research is widely cited across multiple disciplines. Radicchi earned his Ph.D. in Physics from the University of Florence and previously held academic positions in Europe before joining Indiana University. At IU, he teaches courses on network science and data analysis and mentors students in interdisciplinary research. His work integrates physics, data science, and social science to advance understanding of complex interconnected systems and scientific ecosystems.

name: James A. Glazier
title: Professor
research area: Complex Networks; Percolation; Science of Science
short bio: Glazier develops multiscale tissue models (CompuCell3D) with applications in development, immune response, and toxicity. Current efforts include open ecosystems for virtual‑tissue simulation and immunity digital twins.
long bio: James A. Glazier is a Professor of Intelligent Systems Engineering and Biology at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, with additional affiliations in physics and biocomplexity. His research focuses on computational biology, biophysics, and complex systems, particularly the modeling of multicellular systems and biological pattern formation. He is best known for developing the Cellular Potts Model, a widely used computational framework for simulating the behavior of cells and tissues. Glazier directs the Biocomplexity Institute and Initiative (BII) at Indiana University, where he leads interdisciplinary efforts to study biological systems using computational and data-driven methods. His work spans areas such as developmental biology, cancer modeling, tissue engineering, and epidemiology, combining theory, simulation, and experimental collaboration. He has also contributed to the development of CompuCell3D, an open-source modeling environment for simulating multicellular systems. He earned his Ph.D. in Physics from Cornell University and has published extensively in leading journals across physics, biology, and computational science. His research has been supported by agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH). At IU, Glazier teaches courses in complex systems and computational biology and mentors students in interdisciplinary research. Glazier’s work bridges physics, biology, and computing, advancing the understanding of how complex biological structures and behaviors emerge from interactions at the cellular level.

name: Ariful Azad
title: Professor
department: Intelligent Systems Engineering; Director, Biocomplexity Institute
research area: Computational Bio/Multiscale Modeling; Digital Twins in Biomedicine
short bio: Azad designs scalable algorithms/software for massive graphs and GNN workloads. He received DOE Early Career and NSF CAREER awards to build portable graph analytics infrastructure for trillion‑edge networks.
long bio: Ariful Azad is an Assistant Professor of Informatics and Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on high-performance computing, parallel algorithms, and large-scale graph analytics, with an emphasis on processing massive datasets efficiently. He works on designing scalable algorithms and systems for problems such as sparse matrix computations, graph mining, and scientific computing. Azad’s work is particularly known for advancing efficient parallel and distributed methods that can run on modern architectures, including GPUs and large computing clusters. His research has applications in areas such as machine learning, network analysis, and computational biology, where handling large-scale data is critical. He has published extensively in top venues in high-performance computing and data science, contributing both theoretical insights and practical tools. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from Indiana University Bloomington and previously worked as a researcher at institutions including Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, where he contributed to large-scale scientific computing projects. His work has received support from agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF). At Indiana University, Azad teaches courses in data science, parallel computing, and algorithms, mentoring students in cutting-edge research. His work bridges theory and systems, helping enable faster and more efficient computation for data-intensive scientific and engineering applications.

name: Mehmet (“Memo”) Dalkilic
title: Associate Professor
research area: Parallel Graph Algorithms; HPC; Graph ML
short bio: Dalkilic focuses on data mining and applied data science across domains (health, climate, transportation). He has led foundational teaching programs and cross‑disciplinary data efforts on campus.
long bio: Mehmet M. (“Memo”) Dalkilic is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, with an adjunct appointment in Statistics. His research focuses on data science, data mining, and applied artificial intelligence, addressing real-world problems across diverse domains such as astronomy, climate science, bioinformatics, and transportation systems. He works on developing methods for pattern discovery, large-scale data analysis, and predictive modeling, often collaborating across disciplines. Dalkilic is also widely recognized for his contributions to education and curriculum development, having designed and taught foundational courses such as Introduction to Informatics (I101) and developed programs that broaden participation in computing. His teaching emphasizes accessibility, student success, and building strong analytical skills. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from Indiana University Bloomington and has collaborated with organizations such as the Naval Surface Warfare Center on applied data and security problems. His work has been supported by agencies including the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH). At IU, Dalkilic teaches courses in data science and computing fundamentals and mentors students across undergraduate and graduate programs. His work bridges research and education, contributing both to data-driven discovery and to shaping inclusive, impactful computing education.

name: Matthew W. Hahn
title: Professor; Director of Undergraduate Studies (Data Science)
short bio: Hahn’s lab studies evolutionary mechanisms using genomic data, from gene family dynamics (e.g., CAFE) to population genomics and sex‑biased mutation. Work spans *Nature*, *Science Advances*, and leading bioinformatics venues.
long bio: Matthew W. Hahn is a Professor of Biology and Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington, with affiliations in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering and the Department of Biology. His research focuses on evolutionary genomics, bioinformatics, and computational biology, particularly the study of genome evolution across species. He investigates topics such as gene duplication, molecular evolution, phylogenetics, and the evolutionary dynamics of genomes using large-scale genomic data. Hahn’s work combines computational methods, statistical modeling, and evolutionary theory to understand how genetic variation arises and is maintained over time. He has made influential contributions to understanding the evolution of gene families and the reliability of phylogenetic inference. He has published extensively in leading journals such as Nature, Science, and PNAS, and his research is widely cited in evolutionary biology and genomics. He earned his Ph.D. in Biology from the University of Rochester and has received numerous honors, including recognition as a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS). His research has been supported by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH). At Indiana University, Hahn teaches courses in evolutionary biology, genomics, and computational methods, mentoring students across biology and informatics. His work bridges biology and data science, advancing understanding of how genomes evolve and how evolutionary processes shape biodiversity.

name: Chung‑chieh Shan
title: Distinguished Professor
department: Biology & Computer Science; Director, Center for Genomics & Bioinformatics
short bio: Shan develops probabilistic programming languages and program‑transformation approaches to inference, connecting formal semantics with practical ML tooling. Publications span POPL/ICFP/OOPSLA with influential work on continuations and exact Bayesian inference.
long bio: Chung-chieh Shan is an Associate Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on programming languages, probabilistic programming, and the semantics of computation, aiming to develop formal foundations for reasoning about programs and inference systems. He works on topics such as functional programming, program transformations, symbolic inference, and probabilistic modeling, contributing to both theory and practical tools. Shan has made influential contributions to probabilistic programming languages, including techniques for representing and manipulating probabilistic models within programming frameworks. His work bridges computer science, logic, and statistics, enabling more expressive and reliable systems for reasoning under uncertainty. He has published widely in top programming languages and theoretical computer science venues and is an active member of the research community. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from Harvard University and has received recognition for his teaching, including the IU Trustees Teaching Award. Shan co-authored the book Continuations and Natural Language, which connects programming language theory with linguistic concepts. At Indiana University, he teaches courses ranging from introductory programming to advanced topics in programming languages and probabilistic programming, mentoring students in both theoretical and applied research. His work advances the mathematical and conceptual foundations of computing, particularly in areas involving uncertainty and expressive programming systems.

name: Andrew Lukefahr
title: Associate Professor
short bio: Lukefahr studies FPGA and reconfigurable‑system security at circuit/architecture levels and co‑leads SAILIN. The group partners with defense/industry on trusted microelectronics and secure flows.
long bio: Andrew Lukefahr is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on computer architecture and systems, with an emphasis on designing efficient and scalable hardware for modern computing workloads. He works on topics such as memory systems, parallel architectures, and hardware support for machine learning and data-intensive applications. Lukefahr’s research explores how to improve the performance and energy efficiency of computing systems, particularly in the context of emerging workloads like AI and large-scale data processing. He has contributed to the design of novel processor architectures and memory hierarchies, helping address bottlenecks in modern computing systems. His work has been published in top venues in computer architecture such as ISCA, MICRO, and ASPLOS. He earned his Ph.D. in Electrical and Computer Engineering from the University of Texas at Austin and previously worked as a researcher in industry, including at Google, where he contributed to hardware and systems design. His research has received support from agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF). At Indiana University, Lukefahr teaches courses in computer architecture and systems, mentoring students in both undergraduate and graduate research. His work bridges hardware and software, advancing the design of efficient computing systems for next-generation applications.

name: Austin Toombs
title: Victor H. Yngve Distinguished Professor
research area: Information Visualization; Network Science; Data Governance
short bio: Toombs researches sociotechnical communities, making, and care infrastructures, producing sustained CHI/CSCW outputs. He collaborates across HCI/design and AI‑society initiatives.
long bio: Austin Toombs is an Assistant Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on human–computer interaction (HCI), computer-supported cooperative work (CSCW), and workplace technologies, with an emphasis on how people collaborate and coordinate through digital systems. He studies topics such as remote work, teamwork practices, organizational communication, and the design of collaborative tools. Toombs uses qualitative and mixed research methods, including interviews and ethnographic studies, to understand how work practices evolve in modern, technology-mediated environments. His work often examines how tools shape collaboration and how organizations can design systems that better support productivity and well-being. He has published in leading HCI and CSCW venues, contributing to research on the future of work and digital collaboration. He earned his Ph.D. in Informatics from the University of California, Irvine, where he studied collaboration and coordination in distributed teams. Before joining Indiana University, he held academic and research roles focused on human-centered computing and workplace studies. At IU, he teaches courses in interaction design, qualitative methods, and collaborative systems, mentoring students in HCI research. Toombs’s work bridges computing, organizational studies, and design, advancing understanding of how technology can support effective and inclusive collaboration in modern workplaces.

name: Bernard Frischer
title: Associate Professor
short bio: Frischer founded the Virtual World Heritage Lab and led landmark projects in classics/virtual heritage. He continues to publish and advise on policy, standards, and ethics for cultural‑heritage digitization.
long bio: Bernard Frischer is a Professor Emeritus of Informatics and Classical Studies at Indiana University Bloomington, where he was a key figure in the development of digital humanities and virtual heritage research. His work focuses on the application of computing, 3D visualization, and virtual reality to the study of ancient history, archaeology, and cultural heritage. He is best known for pioneering projects that create digital reconstructions of historical sites and artifacts, enabling immersive exploration of ancient environments. Frischer founded and directed the Virtual World Heritage Laboratory (VWHL) at IU, leading interdisciplinary teams that combined archaeology, computer science, and visualization to reconstruct sites such as ancient Rome. His work has been supported by major organizations including the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH). He has also collaborated with museums, research institutions, and international partners to advance digital approaches to cultural heritage preservation. He earned his Ph.D. in Classical Studies and has held academic positions at institutions such as the University of California, Los Angeles before joining Indiana University. Frischer has published extensively on both classical studies and digital heritage methods and has played a leadership role in shaping the field of digital archaeology. His work bridges the humanities and technology, demonstrating how computational tools can transform the study and preservation of the ancient world.

name: Noriko Hara
title: Professor Emeritus; Director Emeritus, VWHL
short bio: Hara studies online knowledge‑sharing and communities of practice, and leads departmental initiatives in ILS teaching and research.
long bio: Noriko Hara is a Professor of Information Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on social informatics, online communities, and information behavior, with an emphasis on how people seek, share, and use information in digital environments. She studies topics such as collaboration in online communities, knowledge sharing, digital participation, and the social impact of information technologies. Hara has conducted influential research on Wikipedia and other online collaborative platforms, examining how contributors interact, resolve conflicts, and sustain participation. Her work also explores barriers to participation, including issues of access, diversity, and inclusion in digital spaces. She has published widely in leading journals in information science and has contributed to understanding how technology shapes social interaction and knowledge production. She earned her Ph.D. in Information Science from Indiana University Bloomington and has received recognition for both her research and teaching. At IU, she teaches courses on information behavior, social informatics, and research methods, mentoring students across disciplines. Hara’s work bridges technology and society, advancing understanding of how digital systems influence collaboration, community, and access to information.

name: Fan Chen
title: Professor; Chair
research area: Social Informatics; Public Engagement with Science
short bio: Chen’s work spans hardware platforms for quantum/AI and efficient computing; listed among AI Center affiliates.
long bio: Fan Chen is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on computer systems, distributed systems, and cloud computing, with an emphasis on building efficient, reliable, and scalable infrastructure for modern applications. He works on problems such as data center systems, resource management, and performance optimization for large-scale distributed environments. Chen’s research explores how to improve the efficiency of systems that support machine learning workloads, big data processing, and cloud services, often designing new techniques for scheduling, storage, and system coordination. His work has been published in leading systems conferences such as USENIX, OSDI, and SOSP, contributing to both theoretical understanding and practical system design. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign, where he specialized in systems and networking research. Before joining Indiana University, he held research positions in both academia and industry, contributing to advancements in cloud infrastructure and distributed computing. At IU, he teaches courses in operating systems, distributed systems, and cloud computing, mentoring students in cutting-edge systems research. Chen’s work bridges theory and practice, advancing the design of high-performance computing systems that power modern data-driven applications.

name: Vikram Jadhao
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Jadhao develops nulloscale modeling tools with applications to materials and energy; affiliate listing with cross‑lab collaborations.
long bio: Vikram Jadhao is an Assistant Professor of Intelligent Systems Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on computational materials science, soft matter physics, and molecular simulations, with an emphasis on understanding complex physical systems at multiple scales. He develops theoretical models and high-performance computational methods to study phenomena such as colloidal systems, polymers, and electrostatic interactions in materials. Jadhao’s work combines physics, engineering, and computation to explore how microscopic interactions give rise to macroscopic material properties. He has contributed to advances in particle-based simulations and scalable algorithms for studying large systems, often leveraging high-performance computing platforms. His research has applications in areas such as energy materials, nullotechnology, and biological systems. He earned his Ph.D. in Mechanical Engineering from Johns Hopkins University and completed postdoctoral research at institutions including the University of Pennsylvania. Before joining Indiana University, he held academic and research positions focused on computational modeling and materials science. At IU, Jadhao teaches courses in computational modeling, thermodynamics, and engineering systems, mentoring students in interdisciplinary research. His work advances the understanding and design of complex materials through physics-based simulation and computational techniques.

name: Paul Macklin
title: Associate Professor
short bio: Macklin leads open tumor/immune modeling frameworks and translational collaborations; affiliate to AI Center.
long bio: Paul Macklin is a Professor of Intelligent Systems Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, with affiliations in mathematics and biomedical engineering. His research focuses on computational biology, mathematical oncology, and multiscale modeling, with a particular emphasis on simulating tumor growth and cancer dynamics. He develops agent-based and continuum models to study how cancer cells interact with each other and their microenvironment. Macklin is best known as the creator of PhysiCell, an open-source physics-based cell simulator widely used to model multicellular biological systems, especially in cancer research. His work integrates mathematics, computer science, and biology to better understand disease progression and to explore potential treatment strategies. He has collaborated extensively with experimental biologists and clinicians to ensure that his models are biologically realistic and clinically relevant. He earned his Ph.D. in Applied Mathematics from the University of Minnesota and completed postdoctoral research at institutions including the Ohio State University. His research has been supported by major agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the National Science Foundation (NSF). At Indiana University, Macklin teaches courses in mathematical modeling and computational biology and mentors students in interdisciplinary research. His work advances the use of simulation and modeling to improve understanding of cancer and support the development of more effective therapies.

name: Amanda Mejia
title: Associate Professor
short bio: Mejia develops statistical methods for brain imaging and contributes to interdisciplinary neuro/AI teams.
long bio: Amanda Mejia is an Associate Professor of Statistics and Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington, with affiliations in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering and the Department of Statistics. Her research focuses on statistical methods for high-dimensional and complex data, particularly in applications to neuroimaging and biomedical data analysis. She develops Bayesian and hierarchical models to better understand brain structure and function using imaging data such as fMRI. Mejia’s work aims to improve the reliability and interpretability of neuroimaging studies by addressing challenges like noise, variability, and multiple comparisons in large datasets. She has contributed to methods for analyzing brain connectivity and spatial-temporal patterns, helping researchers gain insights into neurological and psychological processes. Her research has been published in leading journals in statistics and neuroimaging and has received support from agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH). She earned her Ph.D. in Statistics from the University of Chicago and previously held a faculty position at Indiana University before joining the Luddy School. At IU, she teaches courses in statistics, data science, and Bayesian methods, mentoring students in interdisciplinary research. Mejia’s work bridges statistics, data science, and neuroscience, advancing methods for analyzing complex biological data and improving our understanding of the human brain.

name: Linda Smith
title: Associate Professor
short bio: Smith’s work on infant learning and perception informs computational models of development; AI Center affiliate.
long bio: Linda B. Smith is a Distinguished Professor of Psychological and Brain Sciences and Cognitive Science at Indiana University Bloomington, with strong affiliations to the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on cognitive development, learning, and perception, particularly how infants and young children acquire language, concepts, and knowledge through interaction with their environment. Smith is widely known for her influential work on embodied cognition and developmental systems theory, emphasizing how perception, action, and learning are deeply interconnected. Her research often combines behavioral experiments, computational modeling, and data-driven analysis to understand how complex cognitive abilities emerge from simple learning processes. She has made major contributions to understanding word learning, object recognition, and attention in early development. She earned her Ph.D. in Psychology from the University of Pennsylvania and has received numerous honors, including election to the National Academy of Sciences. Her work has been supported by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH). At Indiana University, Smith teaches courses in cognitive science and developmental psychology and mentors students across disciplines. Her research bridges psychology, neuroscience, and computational modeling, providing foundational insights into how humans learn and develop intelligence.

name: Caleb Weintraub
title: Distinguished & Chancellor’s Professor
short bio: Weintraub explores AI‑assisted creative practice and curation; affiliate listing.
long bio: Caleb Weintraub is an Assistant Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on human–computer interaction (HCI), computer-supported cooperative work (CSCW), and social computing, with an emphasis on how people interact with technology in everyday and community contexts. He studies topics such as online communities, content moderation, digital labor, and the governance of social platforms, exploring how sociotechnical systems shape participation and behavior. Weintraub uses qualitative and mixed methods, including interviews and ethnographic approaches, to understand user experiences and platform dynamics. His work often highlights issues of power, equity, and fairness in digital systems, particularly in how platforms manage user-generated content and labor. He earned his Ph.D. in Information Science from the University of Colorado Boulder and has published in leading HCI and CSCW venues. At Indiana University, he teaches courses in interaction design and social computing and mentors students in interdisciplinary research. His work contributes to designing more equitable, transparent, and human-centered online platforms.

name: Caleb Lucas
title: Associate Professor
department: Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design (AI Center affiliate)
short bio: Lucas models political behavior/opinion dynamics using computational techniques; affiliate listing.
long bio: Caleb Lucas is an Assistant Professor of Political Science at Indiana University Bloomington and an affiliate of the Luddy Artificial Intelligence Center, where he connects computational methods with social and political analysis. His research focuses on computational social science, political behavior, and international relations, particularly how violence, media, and emerging technologies shape public opinion and decision-making. He uses computational techniques such as large-scale text analysis, sentiment analysis, and econometric modeling to study how actors influence civilian attitudes during conflict. Lucas is especially interested in the role of artificial intelligence in political and security contexts, including misinformation and conflict dynamics. Before joining Indiana University, he worked as a political scientist at the RAND Corporation, conducting research for the U.S. Department of Defense. His work has been published in leading journals such as Journal of Politics, International Studies Quarterly, and Political Behavior. He earned his Ph.D. in Political Science from Michigan State University and completed a postdoctoral fellowship at the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research. At IU, he models political behavior and opinion dynamics using computational and data-driven approaches. His work bridges political science, AI, and data science to better understand how technology shapes modern society and conflict.

name: Rachel Hulvey
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Hulvey studies policy/governance of AI globally; affiliate listing.
long bio: Rachel Hulvey is an Assistant Professor at the Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design at Indiana University Bloomington and an affiliate of the Luddy Artificial Intelligence Center, where she works at the intersection of design, emerging technologies, and human-centered systems. Her research focuses on human–computer interaction (HCI), design research, and interactive systems, particularly how design can shape more meaningful and ethical relationships between people and technology. She explores topics such as creative technologies, participatory design, and the social impacts of AI and digital systems, often integrating artistic and design-based methods with computational approaches. Hulvey’s work emphasizes human-centered and speculative design practices, investigating how future technologies can be imagined, critiqued, and responsibly developed. She earned her Ph.D. in Human-Centered Computing from the University of Florida and has a background that blends design, computing, and research. Her work has been presented in leading venues in HCI and design research, contributing to interdisciplinary conversations about technology and society. At Indiana University, she teaches courses in design, interaction, and emerging media, mentoring students across art, design, and computing disciplines. Her work bridges design, AI, and social inquiry, advancing more inclusive and reflective approaches to technological innovation.

name: Gregory Lewis
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Lewis models regulation/control in engineered and social systems; affiliate listing.
long bio: Gregory Lewis is an Assistant Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on artificial intelligence safety, machine learning, and the societal impacts of advanced AI systems, particularly how AI systems can be designed to behave reliably and align with human values. He works on topics such as AI alignment, reinforcement learning, decision-making under uncertainty, and the long-term risks of artificial intelligence, contributing to both theoretical and practical approaches for safer AI. Lewis is especially interested in understanding how increasingly capable AI systems might behave in complex environments and how to mitigate potential risks. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of California, Berkeley, where he worked on machine learning and AI safety. Before joining Indiana University, he was involved in research collaborations and initiatives focused on responsible AI development. His work has been presented in leading AI and machine learning venues and contributes to ongoing discussions about the future of AI governance and ethics. At IU, he teaches courses in machine learning and artificial intelligence and mentors students interested in AI safety research. His work bridges technical AI development with broader societal concerns, aiming to ensure that advanced AI systems are beneficial, reliable, and aligned with human interests.

name: Michael Trosset
title: Distinguished Professor
short bio: Trosset develops theory and methods at the interface of statistics and machine learning, with applications across AI and data science. He contributes to the Luddy AI Center’s ML cluster and graduate training in statistical learning.
long bio: Michael W. Trosset is a Professor of Statistics and Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington, with appointments in the Department of Statistics and the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on statistical computing, multidimensional scaling, and data visualization, with an emphasis on developing computational methods for analyzing complex, high-dimensional data. He is particularly known for his work on distance-based methods and optimization techniques used in statistical modeling and visualization. Trosset has contributed to both theoretical and applied statistics, with applications in fields such as bioinformatics, machine learning, and data analysis. He has published extensively in leading statistics journals and has been involved in advancing statistical software and computational tools. He earned his Ph.D. in Statistics from Ohio State University and has held academic positions at Indiana University for many years. At IU, he teaches courses in statistics, data science, and computational methods, mentoring students across disciplines. His work bridges mathematics, statistics, and computing, contributing to improved methods for understanding and visualizing complex data.

name: Alexandru Georgescu
title: Professor
short bio: Georgescu applies high‑performance computation and ML to problems in theoretical chemistry and materials. His group collaborates with AI Center faculty on scalable modeling and simulation.
long bio: Alexandru Georgescu is an Assistant Professor at the Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design at Indiana University Bloomington and an affiliate of the Luddy Artificial Intelligence Center, where his work bridges design, computation, and emerging technologies. His research focuses on design informatics, computational design, and digital fabrication, exploring how algorithmic and data-driven methods can transform creative practice. He is particularly interested in generative design, parametric modeling, and the integration of AI into architectural and design workflows, investigating how designers can collaborate with intelligent systems to create more adaptive and innovative environments. His work combines design theory with computational tools, addressing challenges in architecture, urban systems, and material fabrication. He has contributed to projects examining how automation and machine learning can augment human creativity while maintaining human-centered design principles. Georgescu earned his Ph.D. in architecture and design computation and has held academic and research positions focused on digital design and advanced fabrication technologies. At Indiana University, he teaches courses in computational design, digital media, and architectural technologies, mentoring students across design and computing disciplines. His work bridges architecture, AI, and design research, advancing new approaches to creativity and technology in the built environment.

name: Kathryn Bonnen
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Bonnen studies human visual processing and perception, combining psychophysics and computational modeling. Her work interfaces with AI/ML methods for understanding visual representations and behavior.
long bio: Kathryn Bonnen is an Assistant Professor of Intelligent Systems Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on computational neuroscience, machine learning, and brain-inspired AI, with an emphasis on understanding how neural systems process visual information. She studies topics such as sensory perception, neural coding, and the relationship between biological and artificial vision systems, aiming to uncover principles that can improve both neuroscience and AI models. Bonnen uses a combination of computational modeling, neural data analysis, and experimental methods to investigate how the brain represents and interprets complex stimuli. She earned her Ph.D. in Neuroscience from New York University and completed postdoctoral research at institutions including Stanford University, where she worked on vision and neural computation. Before joining Indiana University, she held research positions that bridged neuroscience and machine learning. At IU, she teaches courses in neural engineering and computational neuroscience, mentoring students in interdisciplinary research. Her work connects neuroscience, engineering, and AI, advancing understanding of perception and intelligent systems.

name: Joshua Danish
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Danish researches technology‑supported learning and collaborative STEM education. He partners with computing faculty to develop and evaluate AI‑enabled learning environments and analytics.
long bio: Joshua A. Danish is an Associate Professor of Informatics and Learning Sciences at Indiana University Bloomington, with affiliations in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering and the School of Education. His research focuses on learning sciences, educational technology, and embodied cognition, examining how people learn through interaction with physical and digital tools. He studies topics such as STEM learning, computational thinking, and the design of interactive learning environments, often working with children in classroom and informal learning settings. Danish develops and evaluates technology-enhanced learning systems, including simulations, tangible interfaces, and data-rich environments that support inquiry and conceptual understanding. His work emphasizes embodied and multimodal learning, exploring how gestures, physical activity, and interaction with artifacts contribute to understanding complex scientific ideas. He has published extensively in leading learning sciences and educational research venues and has received funding from agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF). He earned his Ph.D. in the Learning Sciences from Northwestern University and has held academic positions focused on interdisciplinary education research. At Indiana University, he teaches courses on learning technologies and research methods, mentoring students across informatics and education. His work bridges computing, education, and cognitive science, advancing how technology can support meaningful and equitable learning experiences.

name: Cindy Hmelo‑Silver
title: Professor
department: School of Education, Instructional Systems Technology (Luddy AI Center affiliate)
short bio: Hmelo‑Silver is a leading scholar in computer‑supported collaborative learning and problem‑based learning. Current projects explore how AI tools can support collaboration, reflection, and assessment at scale.
long bio: Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver is a Distinguished Professor of Learning Sciences at Indiana University Bloomington, with affiliations in the School of Education and the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on learning sciences, problem-based learning (PBL), collaborative learning, and inquiry-based instruction, particularly in STEM education. She studies how students develop deep conceptual understanding, reasoning skills, and the ability to transfer knowledge through collaborative problem-solving environments. Hmelo-Silver is widely recognized for her foundational contributions to problem-based learning, including how instructional design and facilitation support effective learning processes. Her work examines how scaffolding, facilitation, and technology can support students as they engage in complex, authentic tasks. She has also explored how learners build mental models and systems thinking skills, especially in science education contexts. Her research integrates theoretical frameworks with classroom-based studies, making it highly relevant to both researchers and educators. She has published extensively in leading journals in education and the learning sciences and is highly cited in the field. She earned her Ph.D. in Educational Psychology from Vanderbilt University and has held faculty positions at institutions such as Rutgers University before joining Indiana University. Her research has been supported by major funding agencies including the National Science Foundation (NSF). At IU, she teaches courses in learning sciences, research methods, and instructional design, mentoring graduate students and researchers. Hmelo-Silver’s work bridges education, cognitive science, and technology, contributing to improved instructional practices and deeper understanding of how people learn in collaborative, inquiry-driven environments.

name: Laurie McRobbie
title: Distinguished Professor
department: School of Education, Instructional Systems Technology (Luddy AI Center affiliate)
short bio: McRobbie focuses on responsible and ethical AI, bridging policy, governance, and higher‑education perspectives. She contributes to curriculum and campus initiatives on trustworthy AI.
long bio: Laurie McRobbie is an Associate Professor of Learning Sciences at Indiana University Bloomington, with affiliations in the School of Education and the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on science education, inquiry-based learning, and teacher professional development, particularly in K–12 STEM contexts. She studies how teachers design and implement inquiry-oriented and problem-based learning environments that support students’ scientific reasoning and conceptual understanding. McRobbie is especially interested in how classroom practices, curriculum design, and teacher beliefs influence student learning outcomes. Her work also examines how technology and curriculum materials can support effective science instruction and how teachers adapt innovations in real classroom settings. She has contributed to numerous projects aimed at improving science teaching and learning through research-based interventions and professional development programs. McRobbie has published in leading education and science education journals and has been involved in national and international collaborations. She earned her Ph.D. in Science Education from Curtin University in Australia and has held academic positions prior to joining Indiana University. At IU, she teaches courses on science education, curriculum, and research methods, mentoring students in education and learning sciences. Her work bridges education research and classroom practice, advancing more effective and equitable approaches to science teaching and learning.

name: Luyi Xing
title: University Fellow & Adjunct Faculty
short bio: Xing leads research on secure systems and networks, including mobile and IoT security, with emphasis on practical vulnerability discovery and defense. He mentors student CTF teams and contributes to secure‑computing training.
long bio: Luyi Xing is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on computer security and privacy, with an emphasis on identifying vulnerabilities in modern software, web platforms, and mobile systems. She studies topics such as systems security, web security, mobile application security, and network security, aiming to understand how real-world attacks occur and how to prevent them. Xing’s work often combines system-level analysis with data-driven and empirical methods to uncover security flaws at scale. She is particularly known for uncovering practical vulnerabilities in widely used systems, helping improve the security of online services and mobile ecosystems. Her research has been published in top-tier venues such as IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, USENIX Security, and ACM CCS, and is widely cited in the cybersecurity community. She earned her Ph.D. in Computer Science from Pennsylvania State University, where she specialized in systems and security research. Before joining Indiana University, she held research positions focused on cybersecurity and software analysis. Her work has contributed to raising awareness of emerging threats and weaknesses in real-world systems, influencing both academic research and industry practices. At Indiana University, she teaches courses in computer security and privacy, mentoring students in hands-on and research-oriented learning. Xing’s work bridges theory and practice in cybersecurity, advancing the development of secure, reliable, and trustworthy computing systems in an increasingly connected digital world.

name: XiaoFeng Wang
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Wang’s group advances foundational and applied security/privacy, including privacy‑preserving analytics for health/genomic data and large‑scale systems security. He co‑leads SPICE research thrusts across secure computing and privacy.
long bio: XiaoFeng Wang is a Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering and a leading researcher in computer security and privacy. His research focuses on systems security, mobile and web security, data privacy, and applied cryptography, with an emphasis on identifying vulnerabilities in real-world systems. He has made influential contributions to understanding security risks in smartphones, cloud services, and online platforms, often uncovering previously unknown threats and proposing practical defenses. Wang’s work frequently combines system analysis, reverse engineering, and empirical studies to expose weaknesses in widely deployed technologies. His research has led to improved security practices in both academia and industry. He has published extensively in top venues such as IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, USENIX Security, and ACM CCS, and his work is widely cited. He has received numerous honors, including the NSF CAREER Award and multiple best paper awards. He earned his Ph.D. in Information Technology from George Mason University and has held research positions prior to joining Indiana University. At IU, he teaches courses in cybersecurity and mentors graduate and undergraduate students in advanced security research. His work bridges theory and practice, advancing the development of more secure and trustworthy computing systems.

name: L. Jean Camp
title: Professor
short bio: Camp directs SPICE and conducts user‑centered studies of security and privacy, combining behavioral research with systems design. Her team designs usable privacy protocols and investigates phishing, malware, and risk‑incentive mechanisms.
long bio: L. Jean Camp is a Professor of Informatics and Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering and a leading scholar in security, privacy, and the economics of cybersecurity. Her research focuses on usable security, risk communication, and the human and economic factors that influence security behavior, examining how people understand and respond to digital risks. She is known for her work on security decision-making, online safety, and the design of systems that better communicate risk to users, including studies on phishing, authentication, and warnings. Camp’s research integrates computer science, behavioral economics, and public policy, helping bridge technical and societal approaches to cybersecurity. She has published extensively in top venues across security, human-computer interaction, and policy, and her work has influenced both academic research and government practices. She earned her Ph.D. in Engineering and Public Policy from Carnegie Mellon University and has held roles in both academia and policy advisory contexts. Camp has served on advisory boards and contributed to national discussions on cybersecurity and privacy. At Indiana University, she teaches courses on security, privacy, and technology policy, mentoring students across disciplines. Her research has been supported by agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF). Camp’s work advances understanding of how economic incentives and human behavior shape cybersecurity outcomes. Her contributions have helped inform better design of systems and policies for improving online safety and trust.

name: Raquel Hill
title: Professor
short bio: Hill helps lead SPICE efforts on secure computing and health data privacy, connecting policy and practice with secure computation. Her work emphasizes privacy‑preserving sharing and responsible data stewardship.
long bio: Raquel Hill is an Assistant Professor at the Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design at Indiana University Bloomington and an affiliate of the Luddy Artificial Intelligence Center, where her work explores the intersection of design, technology, and social impact. Her research focuses on design, emerging technologies, and critical making, particularly how creative practices can engage with issues of identity, culture, and power in digital systems. She works on topics such as speculative design, interactive media, and the social implications of artificial intelligence, often using artistic and design-based methods to question and reimagine technological futures. Hill’s work emphasizes equity, representation, and inclusion, examining how design can challenge biases and create more just technological systems. She has produced creative and research projects that combine art, design, and computation, contributing to exhibitions and scholarly venues that explore the cultural dimensions of technology. Hill earned her Ph.D. in Design and Media Arts and has a background that blends creative practice with academic research. Before joining Indiana University, she held positions focused on interdisciplinary design and digital media. At IU, she teaches courses in design, media, and emerging technologies, mentoring students across art and computing disciplines. Her work bridges design, AI, and social inquiry, advancing critical and human-centered approaches to technological innovation.

name: Alexander (Alex) Gumennik
title: (Research leader)
short bio: Gumennik develops photonic and fiber‑based intelligent systems that integrate sensing, communication, and AI at the edge. He was recently named an IU Faculty Innovation Ambassador, reflecting translational impact.
