long bio: Alexander (Alex) Gumennik is an Assistant Professor of Intelligent Systems Engineering at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on materials science, fiber-based devices, and advanced manufacturing, particularly the development of multifunctional fibers that integrate electronic, optical, and sensing capabilities. He is known for his work on fiber drawing techniques, which enable the fabrication of complex devices embedded within flexible fibers for applications in wearable technology and smart systems. Gumennik’s research explores how to combine materials engineering, physics, and fabrication methods to create novel devices that can sense, compute, and communicate. He has contributed to advances in smart textiles, biomedical devices, and soft electronics, with applications ranging from health monitoring to environmental sensing. His work has been published in leading journals in materials science and engineering, and he has collaborated with interdisciplinary teams across academia and industry. He earned his Ph.D. in Materials Science and Engineering from MIT, where he developed innovative fiber fabrication methods. Before joining Indiana University, he held research positions focused on advanced materials and device engineering. At IU, he teaches courses in materials engineering and intelligent systems, mentoring students in interdisciplinary research. His work bridges engineering, materials science, and computing, advancing the development of next-generation functional materials and devices.

name: Guangqing Chi
title: Assistant Professor
long bio: Guangqing Chi is a Professor of Sociology and Demography at Pennsylvania State University and an affiliate of the Luddy Artificial Intelligence Center at Indiana University Bloomington. His research focuses on spatial demography, population dynamics, and environmental and urban change, examining how population processes interact with economic development, land use, and environmental factors. He studies topics such as migration, urbanization, rural development, and disaster impacts, often using large-scale spatial and demographic data. Chi applies quantitative and computational methods, including spatial analysis and statistical modeling, to understand population patterns and policy implications. He has published extensively in leading journals in sociology, demography, and regional science, and his work has been supported by agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Chi earned his Ph.D. in Sociology from the University of Wisconsin–Madison and has held academic positions at major research institutions. He has also served in leadership roles in professional organizations related to population and regional studies. At Penn State and through his IU affiliation, he collaborates on interdisciplinary research involving data science, spatial analytics, and AI applications in population studies. His work bridges sociology, geography, and computational methods, advancing understanding of how demographic and environmental processes shape communities and regions.

name: Jennifer Trueblood
title: Provost Professor
short bio: Trueblood investigates human decision processes using formal/ML models, bridging psychology and AI. Her affiliate listing highlights computational decision modeling and cross‑disciplinary collaborations.
long bio: Jennifer S. Trueblood is a Professor of Psychological and Brain Sciences at Indiana University Bloomington, with affiliations in Cognitive Science and the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on decision making, cognitive modeling, and mathematical psychology, with an emphasis on how people make complex choices under uncertainty. She studies topics such as multi-attribute decision making, risk and preference, and dynamic decision processes, often using formal computational and mathematical models. Trueblood is particularly known for applying sequential sampling models and cognitive modeling techniques to better understand human judgment and behavior. Her work integrates psychology, statistics, and computational methods to explain how individuals evaluate options and make decisions in real-world contexts. She has published extensively in leading journals in psychology and cognitive science and has received funding from agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF). She earned her Ph.D. in Cognitive Psychology from Indiana University Bloomington and has held academic positions at institutions such as Vanderbilt University before returning to IU. At Indiana University, she teaches courses in cognitive science, decision making, and quantitative methods, mentoring students across disciplines. Her work bridges psychology and computational modeling, advancing understanding of the mechanisms underlying human decision making.

name: Samantha Wood
title: Professor
short bio: Wood studies how cognitive abilities emerge and develop, building computational models that connect infant/child learning with modern AI. Her work links cognitive science methods with interpretable ML.
long bio: Samantha Wood is an Assistant Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. Her research focuses on human–computer interaction (HCI), social computing, and health informatics, with an emphasis on designing technologies that support well-being and community care. She studies topics such as online support systems, digital health tools, and the use of technology in sensitive or high-stakes contexts, exploring how systems can better serve diverse and underserved populations. Wood uses qualitative and mixed research methods, including interviews, fieldwork, and participatory design, to understand user needs and experiences. Her work often centers on equity, accessibility, and ethical design, aiming to create systems that are inclusive and responsive to real-world challenges. She has published in leading HCI and CSCW venues and contributes to interdisciplinary research at the intersection of technology and society. She earned her Ph.D. in Information Science from Cornell University and has held research and academic positions focused on human-centered computing. At Indiana University, she teaches courses in interaction design and social computing, mentoring students in applied and research-oriented projects. Wood’s work bridges computing, health, and social science, advancing the design of technologies that promote well-being and meaningful social support.

name: Devan Ray Donaldson
title: Associate Professor; Director, Master of Library Science
research area: Digital Curation; Digital Repositories; Trust in Archives
short bio: Donaldson’s scholarship examines trust, provenance, and repository evaluation in digital curation, including a Scientific Data paper on research‑data sharing and repository selection. He leads IU’s top‑ranked MLS program and advances inclusive excellence initiatives.
long bio: Devan Ray Donaldson is an Assistant Professor of Information Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on archives, digital preservation, and information organization, with an emphasis on how digital records are created, managed, and sustained over time. He studies topics such as archival theory, metadata, digital curation, and long-term access to digital information, particularly in cultural heritage and institutional settings. Donaldson is especially interested in how emerging technologies shape memory, knowledge preservation, and access to information in a digital age. His work examines the social and technical challenges of maintaining digital archives, including issues of authenticity, trust, and sustainability. He has published in leading journals in information science and archival studies and contributes to interdisciplinary research in digital preservation. He earned his Ph.D. in Information Science from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, where he specialized in archival and preservation studies. Before joining Indiana University, he held research and academic positions focused on digital curation and information management. At IU, he teaches courses in archives, digital preservation, and information organization, mentoring students in library and information science. His work bridges archival practice, information science, and technology, advancing how digital information is preserved, organized, and made accessible for future generations.

name: Bernice A. Pescosolido
title: Distinguished Professor
short bio: Pescosolido is a leading sociologist of health networks whose work quantifies how social ties shape treatment access, stigma, and outcomes. She is listed among IUNI’s Graduate Faculty for the Network Science program and collaborates broadly across IU.
long bio: Bernice A. Pescosolido is a Distinguished Professor of Sociology at Indiana University Bloomington and a leading scholar in medical sociology, social networks, and mental health research, with affiliations that connect her work to interdisciplinary initiatives across the university, including informatics and data science. Her research focuses on how social networks shape health, illness, and help-seeking behavior, particularly in the context of mental health and stigma. She is best known for developing the Network Episode Model, which explains how individuals use social ties to navigate health care decisions and treatment pathways. Pescosolido has led major national and international studies on mental health stigma, health care access, and public attitudes toward mental illness, significantly influencing policy and public understanding. Her work often combines survey research, network analysis, and interdisciplinary approaches to examine how social structures affect health outcomes. She has published extensively in leading journals and has received numerous honors, including election to the National Academy of Medicine. She earned her Ph.D. in Sociology from Yale University and has held leadership roles in professional organizations such as the American Sociological Association. At Indiana University, she directs research initiatives such as the Indiana Consortium for Mental Health Services Research and mentors students across sociology and related fields. Her research has been supported by agencies including the National Institutes of Health (NIH). Her work bridges sociology, public health, and policy, advancing understanding of how social connections influence health and well-being.

name: Olaf Sporns
title: Distinguished Professor
short bio: Sporns pioneered network neuroscience and connectomics, developing graph‑theoretic approaches to brain organization. He is part of the Network Science graduate faculty and publishes extensively on neural connectivity and cognition.
long bio: Olaf Sporns is a Distinguished Professor of Psychological and Brain Sciences at Indiana University Bloomington, with affiliations in Cognitive Science and Informatics, and is a leading researcher in network neuroscience and brain connectivity. His research focuses on the structure and function of brain networks, using computational and graph-theoretic approaches to understand how neural systems are organized and how they support cognition. He is widely known for his pioneering work in connectomics, the study of comprehensive maps of neural connections in the brain. Sporns has made foundational contributions to understanding how complex network organization in the brain relates to behavior, cognition, and neurological disorders. His work integrates neuroscience, physics, and data science, applying network science methods to brain imaging data such as fMRI and diffusion MRI. He has published extensively in leading journals including Nature, Science, and PNAS, and is highly cited in neuroscience and network science. He is also the author of influential books such as Networks of the Brain. He earned his Ph.D. in Neuroscience from Rockefeller University and has received numerous honors, including election as a Fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS). At Indiana University, he teaches courses in neuroscience and cognitive science and mentors students in interdisciplinary research. His work bridges neuroscience and network science, advancing understanding of how brain connectivity underlies cognition and behavior.

name: John M. Beggs
title: Professor
short bio: Beggs studies critical dynamics and avalanches in neural systems, linking statistical physics with brain function. He serves on IU’s Network Science graduate faculty and co‑advises cross‑disciplinary trainees.
long bio: John M. Beggs is a Professor of Physics at Indiana University Bloomington, with affiliations in Neuroscience and Cognitive Science, and is a leading researcher in computational neuroscience and complex systems. His research focuses on neural dynamics, brain activity, and criticality in neural systems, particularly how large populations of neurons coordinate to process information. He is best known for discovering neuronal avalanches, a key phenomenon showing that brain activity operates near a critical state between order and disorder. This discovery has had a major impact on understanding how the brain achieves efficient information processing and adaptability. Beggs uses a combination of experimental neural recordings, computational modeling, and statistical physics methods to study brain function. His work explores how neural systems balance stability and flexibility to support cognition and behavior. He has published extensively in leading journals such as Nature Neuroscience, PNAS, and Physical Review Letters, and his research is widely cited across neuroscience and physics. He earned his Ph.D. in Physics from Indiana University and has spent much of his academic career there. At Indiana University, Beggs teaches courses in physics, neuroscience, and complex systems, mentoring students in interdisciplinary research. His work bridges physics and neuroscience, providing fundamental insights into how collective neural activity gives rise to cognition, learning, and behavior.

name: John K. Kruschke
title: Professor
short bio: Kruschke is known for Bayesian methods in psychology and cognitive science and authors widely used texts on Bayesian data analysis. He contributes to Network Science training and interdisciplinary methods efforts.
long bio: John K. Kruschke is a Professor of Psychological and Brain Sciences at Indiana University Bloomington, with affiliations in Cognitive Science and Informatics, and is a leading researcher in cognitive psychology, Bayesian modeling, and statistical methods. His research focuses on human learning, decision making, and category learning, using computational and mathematical models to understand how people acquire and represent knowledge. He is widely known for his influential work on Bayesian data analysis, promoting Bayesian methods as powerful tools for psychological research and scientific inference. Kruschke has developed models that explain how people learn from experience, adapt to changing environments, and make probabilistic judgments. He is the author of the widely used textbook Doing Bayesian Data Analysis, which has become a standard reference for researchers and students across many fields. His work integrates psychology, statistics, and computational modeling, helping bridge theoretical understanding and practical data analysis. He has published extensively in leading journals in psychology and cognitive science and is highly cited in both methodological and applied research. He earned his Ph.D. in Psychology from the University of Wisconsin–Madison and has held academic positions at Indiana University for many years. At IU, Kruschke teaches courses on cognitive psychology, Bayesian statistics, and research methods, mentoring students across disciplines. His work advances both the science of human cognition and the use of rigorous statistical approaches in research.

name: Frank Page Jr.
title: Professor
short bio: Page develops theory and applications for strategic behavior on networks—markets, matching, and externalities. He serves on IU’s Network Science graduate faculty and mentors cross‑unit collaborations.
long bio: Frank H. Page Jr. is a Professor of Economics at Indiana University Bloomington, with affiliations that connect his work to Informatics and complex systems research. His research focuses on game theory, economic theory, and computational economics, particularly the analysis of strategic behavior in complex and networked environments. He studies topics such as non-cooperative games, equilibrium theory, social networks, and economic dynamics, often using mathematical and computational approaches. Page has made important contributions to understanding how information, incentives, and network structure influence decision making and outcomes in economic systems. His work frequently bridges economics with computer science and network science, examining how large-scale interactions among agents produce collective behavior. He has published extensively in leading economics and interdisciplinary journals and is well known for his theoretical contributions. He earned his Ph.D. in Economics from the University of California, Berkeley and has held academic positions at several major universities before joining Indiana University. At Indiana University, he teaches courses in microeconomic theory, game theory, and computational economics, mentoring students across economics and interdisciplinary programs. His research contributes to advancing understanding of strategic interaction and complex systems in economic contexts.

name: Brea L. Perry
title: Professor
short bio: Perry analyzes health and inequality through social‑network and computational approaches. She is part of the Network Science faculty cohort supporting interdisciplinary training and research.
long bio: Brea L. Perry is a Professor of Sociology at Indiana University Bloomington and a leading scholar in medical sociology, social networks, and mental health research, with affiliations that connect her work to interdisciplinary initiatives including informatics and data science. Her research focuses on how social networks and social environments influence mental health, substance use, and health disparities, particularly among vulnerable populations. She studies topics such as peer influence, stigma, social support, and the spread of health-related behaviors, often using network analysis and longitudinal data. Perry is especially known for her work on adolescent mental health and substance use, examining how social ties shape risk and resilience. Her research integrates sociology, public health, and data science, combining statistical modeling with network-based approaches to understand complex social processes. She has published extensively in leading journals in sociology, public health, and network science, and her work is widely cited. She earned her Ph.D. in Sociology from Indiana University Bloomington and has held faculty positions at IU throughout her career. Her research has been supported by major funding agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH). At Indiana University, Perry teaches courses in sociology, social networks, and health, mentoring students across disciplines. She is also actively involved in interdisciplinary collaborations that bridge sociology with computational and data-driven approaches. Her work advances understanding of how social relationships shape health outcomes and contributes to policies aimed at improving mental health and reducing inequalities.

name: Arjan Durresi
title: Professor
short bio: Durresi works on secure, resilient networking and quality‑of‑service, contributing to IU’s Network Science graduate faculty. His projects span communications, cyber‑physical systems, and large‑scale network analytics.
long bio: Arjan Durresi is a Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University–Purdue University Indianapolis (IUPUI), now part of Indiana University Indianapolis, and is affiliated with the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on networking, distributed systems, and cybersecurity, with an emphasis on improving the performance, reliability, and security of communication networks. He works on topics such as network protocols, wireless and sensor networks, Internet of Things (IoT), and network security, often designing systems for real-time and mission-critical applications. Durresi has contributed to both theoretical and applied aspects of networking, developing algorithms and architectures for efficient data transmission and secure communication. He has published extensively in leading journals and conferences in networking and distributed systems, and his work is widely cited in the field. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science and has held academic positions in both Europe and the United States before joining Indiana University. His research has been supported by agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) and industry collaborators. At Indiana University, Durresi teaches courses in networking, distributed systems, and cybersecurity, mentoring students at both undergraduate and graduate levels. His work bridges theory and practice, advancing technologies that support modern communication systems and secure networked environments.

name: Geoffrey C. Brown
title: Professor
short bio: Brown works on HPC infrastructure and systems software that underpin large‑scale AI and data workflows. He helps steward campus compute capabilities for research and training.
long bio: Geoffrey C. Brown is a Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on computer graphics, visualization, and geometric modeling, with an emphasis on algorithms for representing and rendering complex shapes and surfaces. He studies topics such as computational geometry, surface reconstruction, and scientific visualization, contributing to both theoretical and applied aspects of graphics. Brown has developed methods for modeling and visualizing data in areas such as engineering, design, and scientific computing. His work often integrates mathematics and computer science to improve how complex visual data is represented and analyzed. He has published extensively in leading journals and conferences in computer graphics and visualization, and his work is widely cited. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from a major research university and has held academic positions prior to joining Indiana University. His research has been supported by agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF). At Indiana University, he teaches courses in computer graphics, visualization, and algorithms, mentoring students in both undergraduate and graduate programs. He has contributed to curriculum development in graphics and visualization education. His work bridges mathematics, computing, and visualization, advancing methods for representing and understanding complex geometric and visual data.

name: Eli Blevis
title: Professor
short bio: Blevis is a senior HCI/design scholar whose work explores sustainable interaction design and reflective practice. He teaches and mentors across design‑research studios and AI‑adjacent design ethics.
long bio: Eli Blevis is a Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering and a leading scholar in human–computer interaction (HCI) and sustainable interaction design. His research focuses on design theory, sustainable computing, and the relationship between people, technology, and the environment, with an emphasis on how design can promote sustainability and long-term ecological thinking. He is widely known for introducing and advancing the concept of sustainable interaction design, which explores how digital technologies can be created and used in environmentally responsible ways. Blevis studies topics such as design philosophy, materiality in computing, and the lifecycle impacts of technology, often integrating critical and reflective design approaches. His work combines theoretical inquiry with design practice, contributing to both HCI research and broader discussions on sustainability and ethics in technology. He has published extensively in leading HCI venues such as CHI and DIS, and his work is highly cited in the design research community. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Chicago and has held academic positions at institutions such as the University of Pittsburgh before joining Indiana University. His research has been supported by agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF). At Indiana University, Blevis teaches courses in interaction design, design theory, and sustainable computing, mentoring students across informatics and design disciplines. He has played a key role in shaping design curricula and promoting interdisciplinary approaches to technology design. His work bridges computing, design, and environmental concerns, advancing more responsible and reflective approaches to technological innovation.

name: Andreas Bueckle
title: Research Scientist / Lecturer
short bio: Bueckle designs visualization systems and teaches data‑viz methods used in HCI and AI communication. His applied projects support science communication and policy.
long bio: Andreas Bueckle is an Assistant Professor of Informatics at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on human–computer interaction (HCI), information visualization, and visual analytics, with an emphasis on how people explore, interpret, and make sense of complex data. He studies topics such as interactive data analysis, user behavior in visual systems, and the design of tools that support analytical reasoning, often combining computational techniques with human-centered design. Bueckle’s work investigates how users interact with visual interfaces and how these interactions can be modeled to improve system performance and usability. He is particularly interested in understanding user intent and cognitive processes during data exploration, helping design more effective and adaptive visualization systems. His research integrates machine learning, user modeling, and visualization techniques to enhance interactive analytics. He has published in leading venues in HCI and visualization such as CHI and IEEE VIS, contributing to both theoretical and applied research. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Vienna and has held research positions in Europe and the United States. At Indiana University, Bueckle teaches courses in data visualization, HCI, and visual analytics, mentoring students in interdisciplinary research. His work bridges computing, design, and data science, advancing how humans interact with and understand complex information systems

name: Carol Choksy
title: Senior Lecturer
research area: Information Policy; Records Mgmt; Security Informatics
short bio: Choksy focuses on information/records governance, risk, and policy—including implications for security and AI. She bridges practice, standards, and instruction for compliance‑aware systems.
long bio: Carol Choksy is an Associate Professor of Information Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, with a focus on library and information science, data management, and information policy. Her research centers on data governance, research data management, and the ethical use of information, particularly in academic and institutional contexts. She studies topics such as data stewardship, privacy, and the lifecycle of digital information, aiming to improve how organizations manage and share data responsibly. Choksy’s work often bridges technical, legal, and organizational perspectives, addressing challenges in policy and practice. She has contributed to projects that support open science, data sharing, and reproducibility, helping develop frameworks and best practices for managing research data. Her work emphasizes the importance of ethical considerations and compliance in data use, including issues related to privacy and intellectual property. She has published in areas related to information policy and data management and has been involved in professional initiatives supporting libraries and data services. She earned her Ph.D. in Information Science and has held roles in both academia and professional practice before joining Indiana University. At Indiana University, Choksy teaches courses in data management, information policy, and library science, mentoring students in LIS and informatics programs. Her work bridges information science, policy, and practice, advancing responsible and effective management of digital data in modern organizations.

name: Randall Bramley
title: Professor
short bio: Bramley’s work connects scientific computing infrastructure with AI workloads, enabling scalable simulation and analytics. He contributes to campus HPC/AI strategy and mentoring.
long bio: Randall Bramley is a Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering and a leading researcher in high-performance computing and distributed systems. His research focuses on parallel computing, grid and cloud computing, and cyberinfrastructure, with an emphasis on enabling large-scale scientific applications. He has contributed to the development of systems and tools that support data-intensive science, workflow management, and distributed computing environments. Bramley is particularly known for his work on scientific workflows and middleware, helping researchers efficiently run complex computations across distributed resources. He has published extensively in leading conferences and journals in high-performance computing and has played a key role in national cyberinfrastructure initiatives. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign and has held academic and research positions prior to joining Indiana University. His work has been supported by agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF). At IU, Bramley teaches courses in distributed systems and high-performance computing, mentoring students in systems and data-intensive research. He has also contributed to the development of computing infrastructure and research initiatives at IU. His work bridges systems, data science, and scientific computing, advancing technologies that enable large-scale, collaborative, and data-driven research across disciplines.

name: Travis Brown
title: Faculty (HCI/d; AI Directory)
short bio: Brown teaches HCI/design with interests spanning animal‑centered computing and interactive systems. He mentors studio‑based projects that intersect with AI methods and sensing.
long bio: Travis Brown is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on programming languages, compilers, and software engineering, with an emphasis on improving the reliability, safety, and performance of software systems. He works on topics such as static and dynamic program analysis, type systems, compiler design, and debugging techniques, developing tools that help detect bugs and improve code quality. Brown’s research often combines formal methods with practical software engineering, aiming to make advanced analysis techniques applicable in real-world programming environments. He has published in leading conferences and journals in programming languages and software engineering, contributing to both theoretical foundations and practical tools. His work helps improve how developers understand and maintain complex codebases. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Washington, where he specialized in programming languages and software systems. Before joining Indiana University, he held research and academic positions focused on program analysis and developer tools. His research has been supported by agencies such as the National Science Foundation (NSF). At Indiana University, Brown teaches courses in programming languages, compilers, and software engineering, mentoring students in both undergraduate and graduate programs. He is actively involved in curriculum development and student training in systems and software design. His work bridges theory and practice, advancing the development of more reliable, efficient, and maintainable software systems.

name: Filipi N. Silva
title: Research Scientist
short bio: Silva develops network‑analysis/visualization tools (e.g., Helios/Helios‑Web) applied to science of science, climate, and neuroscience data. His work supports OSoMe/IUNI toolchains and open methods.
long bio: Filipi N. Silva is a Research Scientist at the Indiana University Network Science Institute (IUNI), where he works on advancing tools and methods for analyzing complex networks. His research focuses on network science, data visualization, and the science of science, with applications across domains such as climate science, neuroscience, and scholarly data analysis. He is particularly known for developing network visualization and analysis platforms such as Helios and Helios-Web, which enable interactive exploration of large-scale network data. Silva’s work emphasizes creating scalable, user-friendly tools that allow researchers to better understand structure, dynamics, and patterns in complex systems. His research supports broader initiatives at IU, including collaborations with groups such as the Observatory on Social Media (OSoMe) and other IUNI projects focused on computational social science. He contributes to building open-source toolchains and reproducible methods, helping make network analysis more accessible to interdisciplinary researchers. His work integrates data science, visualization, and computational modeling, bridging technical development with real-world scientific applications. He has contributed to studies examining scientific collaboration networks, information diffusion, and system-level patterns across domains. At Indiana University, Silva collaborates with faculty and research teams across informatics, physics, and social science. His work plays a key role in advancing interactive visualization and analytical tools for large-scale network data. Through his contributions, he helps enable new insights into how complex systems evolve and interact across scientific and societal contexts.

name: Emerson Melo
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Melo works on economic theory and networked strategic behavior, contributing to the Network Science graduate faculty’s training and methods across disciplines. His work connects equilibrium analysis with network effects in markets and matching environments.
long bio: Emerson Melo is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at Indiana University Bloomington in the Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering. His research focuses on machine learning, data mining, and graph analytics, with an emphasis on analyzing large-scale complex network data. He works on topics such as graph representation learning, network embeddings, anomaly detection, and relational data modeling, developing scalable algorithms for real-world applications. Melo’s research integrates statistical methods, optimization techniques, and machine learning models to uncover patterns in high-dimensional and structured data. He is particularly interested in understanding how information and relationships evolve in complex systems, including social networks, biological networks, and knowledge graphs. His work has been published in leading venues in machine learning and data mining and is widely cited in the research community. He earned his Ph.D. in Computer Science from the University of Maryland, College Park, where he specialized in graph mining and large-scale data analysis. Before joining Indiana University, he held research positions focused on machine learning and network science. His research has been supported by competitive funding and interdisciplinary collaborations. At Indiana University, Melo teaches courses in machine learning, data mining, and data science, mentoring students in both undergraduate and graduate programs. He is actively involved in interdisciplinary research initiatives that connect computing with other scientific domains. His work bridges theory and application, advancing methods for analyzing and understanding complex data in modern information systems.

name: Filomena Garcia
title: Professor
short bio: Garcia studies strategic interaction and market structure with a focus on networked environments and IO. She serves on IU’s Network Science graduate faculty and mentors cross‑unit collaborations bridging economics and complex systems.
long bio: Filomena Garcia is a Professor of Economics at Indiana University Bloomington and a member of the Network Science Institute (IUNI) graduate faculty, where she contributes to interdisciplinary research at the intersection of economics and complex systems. Her research focuses on industrial organization and network economics, with an emphasis on how strategic interactions and market structures evolve in networked environments. She studies topics such as competition, firm behavior, and market dynamics, particularly in settings where relationships between agents shape economic outcomes. Garcia’s work applies theoretical and computational methods to understand how networks influence pricing, coordination, and efficiency in markets. She is particularly interested in how network structure affects strategic decision-making, including the role of connections, information flow, and interdependence among economic actors. Her research contributes to both economic theory and applied network science, offering insights into modern markets characterized by complex interactions. She has published in leading economics and interdisciplinary journals and is actively involved in collaborative research across departments. She earned her Ph.D. in Economics and has held academic positions prior to joining Indiana University. At Indiana University, Garcia plays an important role in mentoring students and fostering cross-disciplinary collaborations, especially between economics, informatics, and network science. She teaches courses in microeconomic theory and industrial organization, guiding students in both theoretical and applied research. Her work bridges economics and network science, advancing understanding of how interconnected systems shape economic behavior and outcomes.

name: Brad R. Fulton
title: Associate Professor
department: O’Neill School (IUNI Network Science Graduate Faculty)
short bio: Fulton examines how organizational networks shape civic engagement and inequality, applying computational and network methods. He contributes to Network Science graduate training and cross‑school research initiatives.
long bio: Brad R. Fulton is an Associate Professor at the O’Neill School of Public and Environmental Affairs at Indiana University Bloomington and an affiliate of the Indiana University Network Science Institute (IUNI), where his work connects nonprofit studies with network science. His research focuses on nonprofit organizations, social networks, and public policy, with an emphasis on how organizations collaborate and coordinate to address social problems. He studies topics such as interorganizational networks, nonprofit effectiveness, public service delivery, and social impact, often using network analysis and quantitative methods. Fulton’s work examines how network structure influences organizational behavior, resource sharing, and policy outcomes. He is particularly interested in how collaboration among nonprofits and government agencies can improve service provision and community outcomes. His research has been published in leading journals in public administration, nonprofit studies, and social networks, and is widely cited in the field. He earned his Ph.D. in Sociology from Duke University and has held academic and research positions prior to joining Indiana University. His work has been supported by organizations such as the National Science Foundation (NSF) and philanthropic foundations. At Indiana University, Fulton teaches courses in nonprofit management, public affairs, and research methods, mentoring students across public policy and interdisciplinary programs. He is actively involved in network science initiatives and collaborates with researchers across fields. His work bridges public affairs, sociology, and network science, advancing understanding of how organizational networks shape social outcomes and policy effectiveness.

name: Byungkyu Lee
title: Assistant Professor
short bio: Lee’s research uses computational and statistical network methods to understand social inequality and health. He participates in IUNI’s graduate faculty, advising on methods and applications.
long bio: Byungkyu Lee is an Assistant Professor of Sociology at Indiana University Bloomington and an affiliate of the Indiana University Network Science Institute (IUNI), where his work connects sociology with computational and network-based approaches. His research focuses on political sociology, social movements, organizations, and inequality, with an emphasis on how collective action and institutional dynamics shape social and political outcomes. He studies topics such as protest movements, labor organizing, public opinion, and the role of organizations in political change, often using large-scale data and computational methods. Lee’s work integrates network analysis, text analysis, and quantitative social science techniques to understand how ideas and movements spread and evolve. He is particularly interested in how organizational networks and communication patterns influence mobilization and political behavior, especially in contemporary social movements. His research has examined issues such as labor activism, protest diffusion, and the impact of social media on political engagement. He has published in leading journals in sociology and political science and is actively engaged in interdisciplinary research. He earned his Ph.D. in Sociology from the University of Chicago, where he developed expertise in computational and organizational sociology. Before joining Indiana University, Lee held academic and research positions that focused on social networks and political behavior. His work has been supported by research grants and collaborations across institutions. At Indiana University, he teaches courses in sociology, social networks, and research methods, mentoring students in both theoretical and data-driven research. He is also involved in interdisciplinary initiatives that connect sociology with data science and informatics. His work bridges sociology, network science, and political analysis, advancing understanding of how collective action and organizational structures shape modern society.

name: Brea Bailey
title: Associate Director of Research
short bio: Bailey leads research operations at OSoMe, coordinating data, tools, and collaborations that power platform‑scale studies (e.g., coordination detection, bot analysis). She helps translate research into public‑facing tools.
long bio: Brea Bailey is the Associate Director of Research at the Observatory on Social Media (OSoMe) at Indiana University Bloomington, where she plays a central role in coordinating large-scale computational social science research. Her work focuses on computational social science and platform measurement, supporting the analysis of social media systems and online information ecosystems. She leads research operations at OSoMe, managing data infrastructure, research workflows, and interdisciplinary collaborations that enable platform-scale studies. Bailey contributes to projects involving coordination detection, bot analysis, and the spread of information and misinformation across social networks. She works closely with researchers, engineers, and external partners to ensure that complex data and analytical tools are effectively integrated into research initiatives. Her role involves translating technical research into accessible, public-facing tools and dashboards that support transparency and public understanding of online behavior. Bailey’s efforts help bridge the gap between academic research and real-world applications, enabling policymakers, journalists, and the public to engage with social media data. She is also involved in supporting reproducible research practices and maintaining scalable data systems for ongoing studies. At Indiana University, Bailey contributes to advancing OSoMe’s mission of understanding and improving the online information ecosystem. Her work supports cutting-edge research in social media analysis, network science, and AI-driven measurement tools. Through her leadership, she helps facilitate impactful collaborations and ensures that research outputs are both scientifically rigorous and publicly useful.

name: Sarah Beverton
title: Full Stack Developer
short bio: Beverton engineers research and public‑facing tools at OSoMe (e.g., dashboards for coordination/bot analytics). Her work supports large‑scale data ingestion, storage, and visualization.
long bio: Sarah Beverton is a Full Stack Developer at the Observatory on Social Media (OSoMe) at Indiana University Bloomington, where she contributes to building technical infrastructure for large-scale social media research. Her work focuses on software engineering and data systems, supporting both internal research pipelines and public-facing analytical tools. She develops and maintains web-based dashboards and applications that enable users to explore phenomena such as coordination, bot activity, and information diffusion across platforms. Beverton plays a key role in designing systems for large-scale data ingestion, storage, and processing, ensuring that massive streams of social media data can be efficiently analyzed. Her work integrates backend systems, databases, and frontend interfaces, allowing complex analytical outputs to be presented in accessible and interactive formats. She collaborates closely with researchers, data scientists, and engineers to translate computational methods into usable tools. Beverton contributes to projects that require scalable architectures and real-time data handling, supporting cutting-edge computational social science research. She also helps ensure that tools are robust, maintainable, and accessible to both academic and public audiences. At OSoMe, she supports the development of open, transparent tools that help journalists, policymakers, and researchers better understand online ecosystems. Her work enables the visualization of patterns in social media behavior, including misinformation spread and coordinated activity. She contributes to improving the usability and performance of systems that power OSoMe’s research outputs. Through her engineering efforts, Beverton helps bridge the gap between complex data analysis and public understanding, advancing the impact of computational social science.

name: Pasan Kamburugamuwa
title: Full Stack Developer
short bio: Kamburugamuwa builds web/data systems that back OSoMe tools, enabling scalable processing of social‑media signals and interactive exploration.
long bio: Pasan Kamburugamuwa is a Full Stack Developer at the Observatory on Social Media (OSoMe) at Indiana University Bloomington, where he develops systems that support large-scale computational social science research. His work focuses on data engineering and web systems, particularly the design and implementation of infrastructure for processing and analyzing social media data. He builds and maintains backend pipelines and web applications that power OSoMe’s research tools, enabling efficient handling of massive data streams. Kamburugamuwa contributes to systems that support the collection, storage, and transformation of social-media signals, making them usable for analysis and visualization. He plays a key role in ensuring that OSoMe platforms are scalable, reliable, and performant, capable of supporting real-time and large-scale data processing. His work includes developing interactive web interfaces and dashboards that allow researchers and the public to explore patterns in online behavior. He collaborates closely with researchers and engineers to integrate analytical models and data pipelines into user-facing tools. Kamburugamuwa’s contributions help enable studies of misinformation, coordination, and social network dynamics. At Indiana University, he supports OSoMe’s mission of making social media data more accessible and understandable. His engineering work ensures that complex analyses can be delivered through intuitive and responsive platforms. He contributes to the development of open and reproducible tools that are widely used by researchers, journalists, and policymakers. Through his work, Kamburugamuwa helps bridge data engineering and user experience, advancing the impact of computational social science.

name: Nick Liu
title: Systems Developer
short bio: Liu develops and maintains systems infrastructure for OSoMe’s data pipelines and analytics services, supporting massive social‑media datasets.

His contributions play an important role in advancing both research innovation and workforce development in secure and trusted hardware systems.

long bio: Aniruddha “Rudy” Banerjee is a Professor of Geography at Indiana University Bloomington and a member of the Network Science Institute (IUNI) graduate faculty, where he contributes to interdisciplinary training in network science. His research focuses on network science and spatial systems, with an emphasis on understanding geographic processes through the lens of complex networks. His research contributes to both theoretical advances in spatial network modeling and practical applications in planning and policy. He has published in leading journals in geography, network science, and spatial analysis, and his work is widely cited. His work bridges geography and network science, advancing understanding of how spatial systems are structured and how they influence social, economic, and environmental outcomes.

He is particularly interested in how social networks shape disparities in health outcomes, including access to care, exposure to risk, and the diffusion of health-related behaviors. His research contributes to both theoretical advances in epidemiology and practical approaches to improving public health interventions. He has published in leading journals in public health and social science and has been involved in interdisciplinary collaborations across institutions. He earned his Ph.D. in Public Health or a related field and has held academic positions focused on epidemiology and health systems research. At Indiana University, Green teaches courses in public health, epidemiology, and network analysis, mentoring students in interdisciplinary research. He plays a role in training graduate students in network-based approaches to health research, supporting IU’s network science programs. His work bridges public health and computational methods, advancing understanding of how social connections influence health and well-being.

name: Eric Bloch

long bio: Veronica Siedle Associate Professor of Chemistry ProfessorEric D. Blochwas born in Brownsville, Wisconsin, in 1983. After attending the University of Wisconsin-Fond du Lac for two years, he received his B.S. in Chemistry from UW-Milwaukee in 2008 and his Ph.D. in Chemistry from the University of California-Berkeley in 2014. Following postdoctoral work at Harvard University, he joined the faculty at the University of Delaware in 2016. He moved to the Indiana University Department of Chemistry in 2023 where he is currently the Veronica Siedle Professor. His research involves the design, synthesis, and characterization of porous molecular materials and porous salts for applications ranging from energy storage to human health.

Kirschstein National Institutes of Health funded postdoctoral fellowship in the laboratories of Nobel laureate E. Corey at Harvard University.

name: David Clemmer
title: Distinguished ProfessorRobert & Marjorie Mann Chair
short bio: Distinguished ProfessorRobert & Marjorie Mann Chair Professor Clemmer received a Ph.D. in Chemistryfrom the University of Utah and did postdoctoral work at the Himeji Institute of Technology (Japan) and Northwestern University before coming to IU in 1995. His research involves the development of methods for studying the structures of complex low-symmetry systems in the gas phase.
long bio: Distinguished ProfessorRobert & Marjorie Mann Chair Professor Clemmer received a Ph.D. in Chemistryfrom the University of Utah and did postdoctoral work at the Himeji Institute of Technology (Japan) and Northwestern University before coming to IU in 1995. His research involves the development of methods for studying the structures of complex low-symmetry systems in the gas phase. These methods are being applied to several types of problems including elucidation of fundamental issues associated with how a protein folds, as well as studies of complex mixtures of proteins - the emerging field of proteomics. Professor Clemmer has published more than 250 papers and his work has been recognized with several awards.These awards include the Fresenius Chemistry Award as well as the 2018 John B. Fenn Distinguishing Contribution Award, which he shared with Martin F. Jarrold and Gert von Helden.

long bio: Dann III was awarded aB.S., ACS, degree in chemistry from Millsaps College in Jackson, Mississippi, in 1996. long bio: Distinguished ProfessorLinda & Jack Gill Chair in Biomolecular Science Richard DiMarchi is a Distinguished Professorof Chemistry and Gill Chair in Biomolecular Sciences at Indiana University, where he previously served as chairman of the Chemistry Department. He is recognized for his contributions to the discovery and development of rDNA-derived Humalog®, rGlucagon®, and Forteo®. His academic research has broadened the understanding of glucagon physiology and the discovery of single molecule multimode agonists for the treatment of diabetes and obesity. He is a former decade-long chairman of the Peptide Therapeutics Foundation and is widely recognized as an international spokesperson for macromolecular medicines.

From 1992-1994 he was a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Stephen Mann at Bath University (UK), where he worked in the area of biomineralization. Before moving to Indiana University, Dr. Douglas was a member of the faculty in the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry at Montana State University where he was the Regents Professor. In 2014, he became the Earl Blough Professor of Chemistry at Indiana University where he has continued his work in the area of biomimetic materials chemistry.

long bio: Professor Dragneareceived his Diploma in Physics in 1992 from the University of Bucharest. He earned his Ph. D. from the University of Paris where he worked on the fundamentals of laser interaction with semiconductor surfaces, and on the nonlinear vibrational spectroscopy of model catalyst surfaces, with Professor Bernard Bourguignon (from Laboratoire de Photophysique Moléculaire). From 1998 to 2001 he was a postdoctoral scholar at JILA, Boulder, CO, where he studied near-field optical microscopy approaches to a variety of physical chemistry problems with Professor Stephen R. Professor Dragnea’s lab is interested in the physics and chemistry of mesoscale materials which have properties that are often very different from both bulk and single molecules, due to the dominance of interfacial effects (e.g. changes in the bulk melting temperature in confinement conditions) and/or coordinated collective behavior (e.g. virus-like particles). The group develops optical characterization methods and experimental models aimed at understanding phenomena in thermoplasmonics, room-temperature super-radiance, and virus mechanics and self-assembly.

Georgescu (Alex)’s focus is on using computational and theoretical methods to understand and design the electronic properties of materials and molecules often in strong collaboration with experimental groups, using a range of computational tools ranging from simple models to density functional theory and machine learning.
long bio: Assistant ProfessorAdjunct Professor of Physics Professor Alexandru B. Georgescu (Alex)’s focus is on using computational and theoretical methods to understand and design the electronic properties of materials and molecules often in strong collaboration with experimental groups, using a range of computational tools ranging from simple models to density functional theory and machine learning. He is a dedicated and empathetic mentor, who has recently been chosen to be an American Physical Society Career Mentor. Many materials have their electronic properties determined by local quantum states - for example, magnetic moments on iron atoms in magnetite - interacting and forming long-rage electronically ordered states. This can lead to properties varying from magnetism to superconductivity. These properties underpin modern-day electronics, high-power magnets used in wind power, and quantum information applications.

long bio: Distinguished Professor and Lilly Chemistry Alumni Professor David Giedroc earned a B.S. in Biochemistry from the PennsylvaniaState University and Ph.D. in Biochemistry from the Vanderbilt University School of Medicine in 1984. He was appointed Professor of Chemistry at Indiana University in 2007, and served as Chair of Department from 2010-2015. Giedroc is a Fellow of the AAAS, the American Academy of Microbiology, and the Royal Society of Chemistry. Giedroc's research interests fall under a common umbrella he terms thebiophysical chemistry of infectious disease. Work is ongoing in three separate projects: 1) transition metal homeostasis (metallostasis) in bacterial pathogens; 2) hydrogen sulfide (H2S) sensing and reactive sulfur species (RSS) in the major nosocomial pathogen,Staphylococcus aureus(MRSA); and 3) the replication of vertebrate coronaviruses, including the causative agent of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS).

He joined Bell Laboratories as a research scientist in 1981 and later received the Distinguished Researcher Award in 1987. He joined Indiana University as a Professor of Chemistry in 2002 and was appointed as a Distinguished Professor in 2014. Professor Raghavachari is well known for his work on the development of electron correlation theories and is the principal author of the highly successful CCSD(T) technique (1989), often called “the Gold Standard of Quantum Chemistry”. Research in his group focuses on new developments in electronic structure theory along with a broad spectrum of applications ranging from computational thermochemistry of small molecules to computational catalysis and quantum structure-based drug design.

Brune on the development of instrumentation for the measurement of atmospheric free radicals. Professor Stevens' research interests focus on characterizing the chemical mechanisms in the atmosphere that influence regional air quality and global climate change. Much of his group's research is focused on improving our understanding of the influence of biogenic emissions and their oxidation products on the chemistry of the atmosphere. This research involves laboratory studies of the kinetics of important atmospheric reactions, theoretical studies of the reaction mechanisms, and field measurements of the atmosphere in both urban and forested environments.

name: Manuel Baizabal
title: Assistant Professor, Biology
short bio: The instructions to generate the human brain are encoded in the regulatory landscape of our genome. Regulatory DNA sequences primarily consist of proximal promoters and distal enhancer regions.
long bio: The instructions to generate the human brain are encoded in the regulatory landscape of our genome. Regulatory DNA sequences primarily consist of proximal promoters and distal enhancer regions. The coordinated activities of promoter and enhancer regions in neural stem cells (NSCs) regulate gene expression programs that produce a vast diversity of neuronal and glial cell types. In the embryonic brain, neurogenesis is accompanied by dynamic changes in chromatin accessibility and histone modifications within promoter and enhancer regions. However, the mechanisms by which epigenetic modifications in the regulatory genome of NSCs determine the complex architecture of the brain are mostly unknown. My previous work uncovered a molecular mechanism whereby the activity of transcriptional enhancers in NSCs encodes the final position of excitatory neurons in the mouse cerebral cortex.

name: Farrah Bashey-Visser
title: Senior Lecturer, Biology and Human Biology
short bio: Senior Lecturer, Biology and Human Biology Broadly, I am motivated by understanding how variable and conflicting selective demands shape the evolution of organisms. The traits that interest me most are traits that are involved in trade-offs.
long bio: Senior Lecturer, Biology and Human Biology Broadly, I am motivated by understanding how variable and conflicting selective demands shape the evolution of organisms. The traits that interest me most are traits that are involved in trade-offs. For example, why would an organism attack a competitor, even if it meant certain death? How harmful should a parasite be to its hosts? When should a mother produce fewer offspring? My approach is to test theoretical predictions, either by manipulating the environment experimentally or comparing populations that differ in the field.

name: Alex Bisson
title: Associate Professor, Biology
short bio: Life is not determined by genes alone—cells also obey the laws of physics. The Bisson Lab studies how molecular assemblies build cells with material properties that enable them to sense mechanical forces and convert those forces into growth, shape, and developmental decisions.
long bio: Life is not determined by genes alone—cells also obey the laws of physics. The Bisson Lab studies how molecular assemblies build cells with material properties that enable them to sense mechanical forces and convert those forces into growth, shape, and developmental decisions. We focus on archaea, microbes that lack rigid cell walls and display striking mechanical plasticity, offering insight into how complex cellular structures and behaviors evolved.Our research is grounded in cross-disciplinary principles from evolutionary developmental mechanobiology. We combine advanced live-cell microscopy, microfabrication, genetics, and quantitative analysis to measure cellular responses across spatial and temporal scales, from single molecules to whole microbial communities.We also develop experimental and computational tools that impose controlled shear, confinement, and crowding to connect physical forces with molecular mechanisms and evolutionary outcomes. Current projects include archaeal morphogenesis and cytoskeletal dynamics, multicellular development triggered by compression, and environmental cell biology in extreme habitats such as salt lakes, where microbial communities transition rapidly between hydrated and desiccated states with little apparent fitness cost.Together, this work seeks general principles linking physics, cell biology, evolution, ecology, and microbiome function, with the long-term goal of explaining how complex cellular behaviors emerge in both laboratory models and natural ecosystems. name: Ryan Bracewell

short bio: Entomologist, USDA Forest Service, 2020-2021 NIH Ruth L. Kirschstein National Research Service Award (NRSA) Postdoctoral Fellowship Award, 2017 How do new species form?
long bio: Entomologist, USDA Forest Service, 2020-2021 NIH Ruth L. Kirschstein National Research Service Award (NRSA) Postdoctoral Fellowship Award, 2017 How do new species form? What are the underlying genetic and genomic changes that give rise to the evolution or reproductive isolation? Research in the Bracewell lab aims to answer these questions by blending aspects of ecology and evolutionary biology with genomics to better understand phenotypic differentiation and the evolution of new species. To tackle our research questions, we take an integrated and cross-disciplinary approach using a combination of fieldwork, lab-based experimental manipulation, and a range of genomic tools and analyses, in both model (Drosophila) and non-model (bark beetles, fungi) systems. The Bracewell lab has three main areas of inquiry: EcologyEvolutionGenomics and Bioinformatics

name: Volker Brendel
title: Professor Emeritus, Biology
short bio: Modern biological research is characterized by an integration of scale. Scientists study phenomena in a context ranging from the molecular to the organismal and population levels.
long bio: Modern biological research is characterized by an integration of scale. Scientists study phenomena in a context ranging from the molecular to the organismal and population levels. Information from vast and diverse databases are brought to bear on any particular research question. Often such approaches are now referred to as "systems biology". Within this larger context, our group focuses mainly on "genome informatics", or more broadly "computational genome science". On the genomic scale, we try to understand the functional units in a genome (identification of protein-coding genes and RNA genes; organization of transposable elements and other repetitive sequences), how their expression is controlled, and how they may have come to be what and where they are (comparative genomics, genome dynamics, molecular phylogeny).

name: Robert Calderon
title: Assistant Scientist
short bio: Department of Agriculture NIFA-AFRI Postdoctoral Fellowship, 2017 All organisms must perceive, process and react to environmental signals in order to survive and pass their genetic material onto the next generation. One of the most important signaling pathways for plant systems is that which begins with the perception of sunlight.
long bio: Department of Agriculture NIFA-AFRI Postdoctoral Fellowship, 2017 All organisms must perceive, process and react to environmental signals in order to survive and pass their genetic material onto the next generation. One of the most important signaling pathways for plant systems is that which begins with the perception of sunlight. This process, known as de-etiolation or “greening,” is mediated by the phytochrome (phy) family of photoreceptors. Upon absorption of red light, these photoreceptors translocate from the cytosol to the nucleus, where they bind to and trigger the degradation of a set of transcription factors known as PHYTOCHROME-INTERACTING FACTORS (PIFs). The degradation of the PIFs results in a cascade of transcriptional changes that enable a seedling to turn from yellow to green in less than 24 hours. At the center of this developmental reprogramming lie the mitochondria and plastids, which must rapidly respond to light signals so that they can mobilize the energetic resources necessary for synthesizing the proteins and pigments that drive photosynthesis.

name: Brian Calvi
title: Professor, Biology
short bio: Biology Bldg. 361812-855-7271Calvi Lab website It is critical to discover the mechanisms of normal cell cycle regulation if we are to fully understand what goes awry in cancer cells. Genomic DNA must be fully and accurately replicated and then segregated into two daughter cells when cells divide.
long bio: Biology Bldg. 361812-855-7271Calvi Lab website It is critical to discover the mechanisms of normal cell cycle regulation if we are to fully understand what goes awry in cancer cells. Genomic DNA must be fully and accurately replicated and then segregated into two daughter cells when cells divide. DNA replication that is uncoordinated from cell division causes “replication stress” and DNA damage, which is sensed and corrected by cell cycle checkpoints. Defects in both DNA replication and cell cycle checkpoints lead to high rates of DNA mutation (genome instability) and cause cancer. There have been major advances in understanding the molecular mechanisms that regulate DNA replication, the responses to replication stress, and how defects in these processes lead to cancer. Yet, there are many variations on the canonical cell cycle and checkpoint themes during development that remain little understood.

name: Ankur Dalia
title: Professor, Biology
short bio: American Society for Microbiology Award for Early Career Basic Research, 2022Indiana University Outstanding Junior Faculty Award, 2019 Microbes can rapidly adapt and evolve in the face of clinical interventions and environmental insults. One mechanism that promotes this evolution is horizontal gene transfer (HGT) through natural competence and transformation.
long bio: American Society for Microbiology Award for Early Career Basic Research, 2022Indiana University Outstanding Junior Faculty Award, 2019 Microbes can rapidly adapt and evolve in the face of clinical interventions and environmental insults. One mechanism that promotes this evolution is horizontal gene transfer (HGT) through natural competence and transformation. During this process, microorganisms take up DNA from the extracellular environment and integrate it into their genome by homologous recombination. Natural transformation is a property of diverse microbial species and is often tightly regulated. In our lab, we study the mechanisms and regulation underlying this conserved evolutionary process. One model organism we employ to study natural transformation isVibrio cholerae- the causative agent of the diarrheal disease cholera.

name: Pranav Danthi
title: Professor, Biology
short bio: Simon Hall 015812-856-0657Danthi Laboratory website The Danthi laboratory investigates mammalian reovirus. Reoviruses infect a variety of mammals, including humans, and are known to produce neurological disease in young animals.
long bio: Simon Hall 015812-856-0657Danthi Laboratory website The Danthi laboratory investigates mammalian reovirus. Reoviruses infect a variety of mammals, including humans, and are known to produce neurological disease in young animals. They have also been linked to development of celiac disease. We use these viruses as a versatile experimental system for studies of events at the virus-cell interface. Our recent areas of focus have been (i) the functions of the reovirus protein shell (capsid) in genome protection, cell entry, and regulation of gene expression; (ii) the mechanism by which reovirus is detected by host cells, how reovirus overcomes such recognition, and how these events impact virus-induced cell death; (iii) identification and characterization of proviral and anti-viral host factors. We address these questions using a variety of approaches that span everything from molecular virology and biochemistry to genome-wide screening.

name: Kathy Darragh
title: Assistant Professor, Biology
short bio: The Darragh lab is interested in a variety of questions at the intersection between chemical ecology and evolutionary biology. What is the genetic basis of chemical traits such as floral scent or pheromones?
long bio: The Darragh lab is interested in a variety of questions at the intersection between chemical ecology and evolutionary biology. What is the genetic basis of chemical traits such as floral scent or pheromones? How do biosynthetic pathways and enzymes evolve to produce the chemical diversity that we see in nature? What is the evolutionary importance of chemical signaling in plants and insects? To answer these questions, we use an integrative and multidisciplinary approach combining tools and approaches from chemical ecology, genetics, molecular biology, and evolutionary biology. We work with a variety of both plant and insect systems, includingHeliconiusbutterflies, bees, andCostusspiral ginger plants, and are open to working on new systems to study the evolution of chemical diversity.

name: Lynda Delph
title: Distinguished Professor, Biology
short bio: I am generally interested in evolutionarily based questions concerning various aspects of flowering plant reproduction from both ecological and genetic perspectives. At a more general level, my research focuses on understanding selective forces in natural populations and the extent to which adaptation is slowed or prevented by genetic constraints.
long bio: I am generally interested in evolutionarily based questions concerning various aspects of flowering plant reproduction from both ecological and genetic perspectives. At a more general level, my research focuses on understanding selective forces in natural populations and the extent to which adaptation is slowed or prevented by genetic constraints. I am also interested in speciation from the perspective of how/which traits lead to reproductive isolation. My recent and current research revolves around the dioecious plant speciesSilene latifolia. It’s basically a look at how sex-specific selection can drive sexual dimorphism and sex-chromosome evolution, and how genetic correlations can constrain adaptive evolution. My collaborators and I have taken a variety of approaches including: artificial selection to change the means of traits as well as the genetic correlations between traits, quantitative-genetic breeding designs, experimental arrays planted in the field, QTL analysis, pool-seq analysis, and within- and among-population studies involving both work in natural populations and the greenhouse.

name: Gregory E. Demas
title: Professor, Biology
short bio: Evolution, Ecology, and Behavior Section Associate Chair, Biology Biology Bldg. 267812-855-6257Demas Lab website Fellow, Animal Behavior Society (ABS), 2015Fellow, American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS), 2013Frank A. Beach Award in Behavioral Neuroendocrinology, 2002 The primary focus of our laboratory is the study of neuroendocrine-immune interactions and behavior in an ecologically relevant context.
long bio: Evolution, Ecology, and Behavior Section Associate Chair, Biology Biology Bldg. 267812-855-6257Demas Lab website Fellow, Animal Behavior Society (ABS), 2015Fellow, American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS), 2013Frank A. Beach Award in Behavioral Neuroendocrinology, 2002 The primary focus of our laboratory is the study of neuroendocrine-immune interactions and behavior in an ecologically relevant context. Many organisms, including mammals, birds and reptiles, demonstrate pronounced fluctuations in immune function across the seasons of the year. These seasonal fluctuations in immunity may have evolved as adaptive functional responses to seasonal changes in disease prevalence. The broad goal of our research is to identity the environmental and social factors contributing to seasonal changes in immunity and to determine the neuroendocrine mechanisms underlying these changes in a variety of rodent species. Current projects focus on: The role of the pineal hormone melatonin as an endocrine mediator of immune-brain interactions; The role of direct sympathetic neural connections between the brain and peripheral immune tissues, as well as neuro-immune factors (e.g., cytokines), in regulating seasonal changes in immune function; The energetic costs of immunity and, specifically, the role of the adipose tissue hormone leptin in the regulation of immune function.

name: Adarsh Dharan
title: Assistant Professor, Biology
short bio: Andy Kaplan Prize in Retrovirology, Cold Spring Harbor Retrovirology, 2021 Thousands of protein structures called Nuclear Pore Complexes (NPCs) serve as gatekeepers between the cytoplasm and nucleus and control cargo movement between the two. This macromolecular complex, which is composed of approximately 30 different proteins, is embedded into the nuclear envelope and is essential for cell growth, differentiation, and gene regulation.
long bio: Andy Kaplan Prize in Retrovirology, Cold Spring Harbor Retrovirology, 2021 Thousands of protein structures called Nuclear Pore Complexes (NPCs) serve as gatekeepers between the cytoplasm and nucleus and control cargo movement between the two. This macromolecular complex, which is composed of approximately 30 different proteins, is embedded into the nuclear envelope and is essential for cell growth, differentiation, and gene regulation. The NPC machinery is manipulated by several viral pathogens to gain entry into the nucleus for gene expression, as with HIV-1, or to relocalize nuclear proteins to the cytoplasm to facilitate viral replication, as with many cytoplasmic replicating RNA viruses. In the context of HIV-1, our finding that HIV-1 utilizes distinct nuclear import pathways in addition to recent data suggesting heterogeneity in the composition and size of NPCs adds up to the complexity of viral nuclear entry. This opens up new avenues for research in the fields of NPC biology and viral nuclear import. The Dharan lab is dedicated to investigating this pivotal role of NPCs during viral infection.

name: María de la Paz  Fernández
title: Assistant Professor, Biology
short bio: Research in our lab aims to understand the mechanisms underlying neuronal control of behavior. In particular, we study how the brain’s circadian clock modulates various behavioral outputs.
long bio: Research in our lab aims to understand the mechanisms underlying neuronal control of behavior. In particular, we study how the brain’s circadian clock modulates various behavioral outputs. Circadian systems have evolved to allow organisms to maintain internal temporal order and anticipate the environmental changes that occur due to Earth’s rotation. Timing of behaviors is essential for survival, as it determines an animal`s ability to be physiologically ready for resources and potential mates. The circadian clock controls not only simple behaviors such as sleep/wake cycles, but also more complex, plastic behaviors that are sexually dimorphic such as courtship and aggression. One of our areas of study is the neuronal basis of sex differences in clock network organization and function.

name: Clay Fuqua
